NOTHING Mean About Him—The extremist. A WOMAN is sometimes minded better when she iSn't strong minded. No one eau define love, although we all know it 3 by heart. A man never realises his worth until he is sued
for breach of promise. WHEN a woman's face is her fortune, old age

sends her into bankruptcy. "THERE is no place like home," provided it isn't one where you are labelled an "inmate." FAVOUR is one of those things which you can best keep in by asking for none of it. LEISURE is the condition in which you have to work hard without pay in order to kill the time. A COUNTRY village is the best place for the young fellow who wants to be a "prominent mer• chant." .
CAPITAL ' CHAT.

The confidence which city men repose in Lord Rosebery was shown a few nights ago by the ban- quet given to him by the City Liberal Club. Al- though the club takes the name of LiberaLand there- fore identifies itself with a political side, upwards of half its members are Liberal Unionists, and its ' political character is therefore neutralised. It has come to be little else than a social institution, and 1 is of admirable convenience to city men as: a general lunci.ing centre. The city Liberal Unionist is a man of Imperial ideas, and knows on which side his business interests li. He would accordingly join the purely tiladstonian members in giving a hearty reception to a Prime Minister who is the very embodiment of Imperialism ; and so the eve - ing passed off in the most perfect good humour. Everybody was completely at his ease, as the ban- quft, was quite a private one.

There is no exaggerating [lle unpleasant sensa- tion which Mr. Chamberlain's letter on the subject of Welsh Disestablishment has caused amongst the Conservatives, and especially in the ranks of the Church party. Such a declaration was totally un- looked for, and the moment chosen for publishing it has increased its effect tenfold. If in the middle of the recess lr. Chamberlain bad chosen to express an opinion in favour of Welsh Disestabflshment in the abstract, his Conservative friends would still have thought the declaration uncalled for ; but the fact that he has chosen the very eve of the session to write a strongly worded letter which practically gives away the Welsh case against the bill is regarded as susceptible of only one interpretation— that it is a distinct betrayal of the Unionist alliance at a critical moment. If Mr. Chamberlain can act like this on the Welsh Disestablishment Bill, what proof is there, the Con- servatives are asking, that he can be cotnted on to help them in opposing the Registration Bill and the other Government measures of th,.. old fashioned Tories are nature . in the matter, bee,ause they bal Mr. Chamberlain ; and with thi s ao" told you so." Putting the extr of "be- trayal " out of the question, the,-. . another explanation which, while more i is scarcely more reassuring to the Oppositic •.- known, of course, that Mr. Chane. of his followers were not soun and that they were extremely in conse- quence to prevent the bill from being read a second time. But it has always been understood that Mr. Chamberlain was satisfied of the ability of the Op- position to prevent this stage from beiig reached by a cotip at the beginning of the session. But if his letter is intended to explain away his action in regard to the bill beforehand, it is plain that he must now have abandoned all hope of tliis.

Like Lord Rosebery, the father of the present Lord Derby had a great longing to add to the honour of being Prime Minister that of winning the Derby. Once he felt quite confident of success. It was in 1858 when his colt Toxophilit e started a hot favourite. But Sir Joseph Hawley had a better horse in Beadsman, who won comfortably by a length, Toxophilite being second • Both horses had a distinguished stud care Jr. Beadsman became father of such famous animals as Blue Down, Green Sleeves, Rosicrucian, anc4 Pero Gomtz. It may here be remarked that Sir Joseph Clawley, com- monly known as "the lucky baronet," bought Mendicant,the dam of Beadsman, for what was then deemed the ridiculously high price of 3,000 guineas. But with Mendicant's sons and grand- sons he won in stakes and bets nearly half a million of money. Toxophilite earned his fame in a less direct way. His son Musket was sent out to Australia, where be may be said to have founded the breeds of Australian thoroughbreds. He has been in sport the Eclipse of the Antipodes.

__— His most distinguished representative. Carbine, has now been bought by the Duke of rt'ortland and will shortly arrive in England. The experiment I will be watched with the deepest interest by all who care for horse breeding, lany good judges have long thought that the English racehorse is slightly deteriorating in wind and a robust con- stitution ; and Count Lehndorff, one of the greatest authorities on horse breeding, wrote several years ago that we wanted an infusion of tresh blood. Now, the Musket breed are celebrated for their staying power and strong health, and so with the arrival of Carbine quite a new departure may proh- ab'y or possibly be made with regard to our thorough-breds. It is noteworthy that Quiver,who is so nearly an own sister to Musket, the slightest variance in relation is scarcely worth csnsiderstion, has in Memoir and La Fleche produced two of the best mares of modern years.

I wrote Another man's name on a cheque, and got caught because I hadn't spelled it right." BEYOND HOPE.— This," said the attendant, as he led the way through the incurable ward, "is one of the worst eases we have. He was once newspaper man." "But what is his hallucina- tion ? ' asked the visitor' anxiously. "He thinks he has money," answered the attendant, sadly. A FEW years since, at the celebration of a national anniversary, a poor pedlar who was pre- sent, being asked for a toast, gave the following : "Here's a health to poverty ; it sticks to a man when all his friends have deserted him." There was a chance of Lord Russell's court in the Palace of Justice on Tuesday providing much more interesting reading for th'e public than the debates in Parliament. A breach of promise case, Wynd- ham versus Viscount Deerburst,was down for bear- ing, being a claim against the eldest son of the Earl of Coventry, who last year mar- ried the daughter of an American millionaire. The court was crowded, and as the defendant bad all along let it be known that he meant to fight the matter out, as the pleadings indicated some sensa- tional disclosures, and as it was said 400 letters had passed between the parties, expectation was at its height. But the plaintiff did not put in an appear- ance, and, as without her nothing could be done to advance her claim, a verdict was given for the defendant, and judgment entered for him.

The licensed victuallers are about to enter upon a great campaign in defence of their interests. As the policy of the Liberal Government is supposed to be inimical to those interests, their propaganda will be directed to the return of Conservative members both for the London County Council and Parliament. Candidates will he subjected, not to a political, but to a trade test. Nominally there will be no party lines in the campaign, ani a Liberal who is sound upon the question of compensation will have as great a chance,according to the leaders of the campaign, as a Conservative. They will not find many Liberal candidates willing to commit themselves to a vote against their party ; and if they did,theLiberal candidates so committing them- selves would not find many Liberal electors to give them support. Whatever non-party complexion, therefore, may be given to the movernent,it will be nothing but an attempt to place the Conseryatives in power. The trade will prefer their self-preser- vation to joining in an attack on the House of Lords. A manifesto will immediately be issued,and a Aeries of test questions prepared for every can- didate ; and the trade and their friends will be worked with the same enthusiasm and thorough- ness with which the Temperance leaders keep their hand upon their supporters.

The amendments on the Address are already numerous. The one relating to agricultural depres- sion is in the hands of Major Rasch,the unemployed one in those of Dlr. Keir Hardie,and the Redmonditee have a triplet. Major Nolan will move one on the famine in the West, Mr. Clancy one on the amnesty of prisoners, while Mr. Redmond, by demanding an instant appeal to the country on Home Rule, will give Mr. Balfour an opportunity to fulfil his promise to vote for anything that will compel an early appeal to the country. I‘l r. Broadhurst has also an amendment in favour of confering old-age pensions on all persons above sixty years of age. The debate on the Address thus promises to be protracted.

The Carlyle fund is accumulating very slowly ; not nearly the sum required to purchase the free- hold of his house has yet been raised. But it is about to receive the imprimatur and blessing of the Mansion House, where a meeting is to be held at the end of the month for the purpose of pushing it into notice. Had the movement been possible a quarter of a century ago, when Carlyle was in the zenith of his fame and influence, the amount needed would easily have been obtained. Or if half the private letters that he wrote had been left unwritten, there would have been infinitely lest difficulty than there is about getting the money; but he has been in a great measure the author cf his own unpopu- larity, and it will require a good deal of begging before his old dwelling place can be made fit to re- ceive a single visitor.

Porous glass window-panes are being made in Paris. The minute holes in the glass are too fine to permit of a draught, and yet large enough to afford a pleasant and healthy method of ventilation. Miss White, a pupil teacher at Shrewsbury, showed great courage in saving a little girl, a pupil at St. Mary's Board School, who had been sliding on the canal, and had fallen into the water. This is not the first time Miss White has been the means of saving life.

HAMLET. The hour dreaded by Geoffrey Trevelyan and the Lady Beatrice for eighteen years had come at last.
Children's Dress.

Their enemy had found them out 1 Their secret was discovered ! At the sight of Lord Trevelyan, with his blazing eyes, and wild face pale with fury, the Lady Beatrice uttered a startled cry, and dropping Fay, she clung to her husband with the evident determination that death alone should separate

The serge or homespun school frocks are now supple- mented with blouses of Alpine wool in the daintiest , colourings, with elongated dots or narrow stripes figured • in white upon its surface and relieved with velvet rib- bons. A pretty pale blue-and-white blouse had a broad pleat down the front fastened with pearl studs, the ful- ness at each side drawn in lines at the collar, the broad waist-belt finishing the blouse at the waist, large full sleeves fastened in front of the arm from wrist to elbow. A velvet ribbon in a pretty shade of moss-green formed the neck band, fastening in a square bow at the back of the neck, and a girdle of ribbon passed around- the armhole and continued to the centre of the waist at the back, where it fastened to the skirt in a bow, a most.. sensible arrangement,as it eased the weight of the heavy skirt—winter clothing is always weighty—from the waist to the shoelders, as it always should be arranged for delicate or growing children. --- What Blind Folk Dream: Visions in Remarkable Forms. "Do you ever dream? and if so, what do you dream about? "I asked a blind man a little while ago (writes a representative of " Cassell' s Saturday Journal ''). "Ys," he answered, " Ido dream occasionally; but ft is very rarely that I do so; only when I have had a heavy supper, in fact. I may dream of a lot of differ- ent things then: perhaps of my brothers and sisters; but they always appear as little girls and boys, dressed in the.fashion of sixty years ago—for I myself am nearly seventy years of age, and have been blind ever since I was six years old : lost my sight through an attack of smallpox. My youngest brother must be considerably over sixty now; but I can only think of him as a baby in long clothes, and I dream of him like that—though I must say that it seems funny to think of a baby being a prominent member in the Steck Exchange. Dream of other things? Oh, yes. I dreamt only last night that I was playing in the fields outside my native village in Gloucestershire ; but those fields are no Langer there. Occasionally I have what I call abstract dreams—that is, I dream, for examp'e, that I am selling matches in the street ; but it is very hard to describe, for I don't see either myself or the street in the dream. I only know that I am there in the same way as I know I am here. In fact, I dream an idea. But if ever Ido dream of myself, and not of the idea of myself—if you can understand what I mean—l arn always a little boy wito golden hair, and a lace collar round my neck." The writer spoke to several other blind persons, both male and female, who had had their eyesight within their memories, but few of them ever dreamed at all, either materially (I call a material dream one in which the dreamer actually sees what he dreams in his mind's eye) or abstractly ; whilst others who did, and were able to put their ideas into words, told me much the same as the above-mentioned interviewee. When at last I came across a case who had a sufficient flow of language to be able to express her meaning, I found that her dreams were all of the abstract variety. She said—" You know, I have not the slightest idea of shape beyond what I can get through my fingers. I can't imagine what anything is like at all, for I don't know what seeing is. All I can do is to recognise by my touch a thing which I have touched before, or something similar to a thing I have touched before. I seldom dream, but when I do, I dream of a lot of different things. I have, for instance, dreamed of colour—at least, I think it is colour ; but I do wish that I could oisly see such a thing for a moment, just to make sur• that my conception of it is something likethe real thing. Well, I'll tell you what my idea of colour is if you like ; hut you musn't laugh at me. It is a kind of a sound. Thus, a low doleful note on the organ means black to me ; a loud, jarring sound is red ; and white is one of the high soft notes of the human voice. In fact, every note to me represents a colour. All the more strikiug colours as you describe them—such as you call red, yel- low, green—are given by harsh sounds ; and all the quiet ones, heliotrope for instance—that's my favourite colour, because of the smell—or blue-grey are given by soft and flute-like notes." Those blind people who are . naturally musical usually dream of something in con- nection with music—dream through their ears, in fact. One young fellow to whom I spoke is of 'a genius and a fine performer on the organ, and one night not long ago dreamt a tune. When he awoke in the morning he re- membered it, and played it on the organ. It was scored by a musican living in the neighbourhood, and is really a very fine piece of music.

them. "Officers !" cried Lord Trevelyan, his words ringing out like a battle cry, "I charge this man, Geoffrey Trevelyan, with robbery and intent to murder me, eighteen years ago. Arrest him!" The officers advanced to obey the command. The Lady Beatrice put out her slender hand to ward them off. "Hush, Beatrice !" said her husband, gently, and with infinite tenderness, more thoughtful of her than of himself in that supreme moment. "It shall all be well with us. Pernaps it is better. after all, that all our anxieties, our life of secrecy and watchfulness, should be ended. My darling let me go. Spare yourself and our chil- dren.' The Lady Beatrice looked around her wildly. Her straying glance caught her father's cold stern face, now pale and shocked in its expression. "Father 1" she cried, appealing to him with a passionate voice, "you hear? You see what they would do with Geoffrey? Father, for seventeen years I have been in secret Geoffrey Trevelyan's wife. These are my children and his," and she looked around on her three children with burning eyes—" your grandchildren. father ! Plead for them and me ! I shall die if they take him from me—my Geoffrey—m} husband ! " Was this impassioned creature the Lady Beatrice? Even in his anguish the earl won- dered. "Grand papa, plead for him!" cried Fay, sobbing wildly. "Save my papa ! " The sweet voice, the anguished words, went to Lord Hampton's heart. "Trevelyan," he said, tears in his eyes, hasn't this gone far enough? After all. Geoffrey was but a boy eighteen years ago. For my daughters sake—for the sake of our old iriendship—for the sake of.--of my innocent grandchildren—let him go! The marquis sneered. "Not though an angel pleaded for him!" he ejaculated. Giralda sprang forward and knelt at his feet, her sweet face upturned to his in agonized plead- ing. "Uncle Trevelyan' withdraw your charge for my sake," she said, brokenly. For an instant the marquis wavered. But Lord Adlowe, standing at his elbow, whispered in his ear a repetition of the falsehoods he hat uttered before concerning Giralda's pretended scorn, and the old lord hardened his heart against her. "You may as well plead to a rock as plead to me 2" he cried. "Officers, do your duty. I de- mand only justice—and I will have justice 2" The officers moved upon their victim. For a moment a wild scene reigned—the wife's shrieks, the daughter's moans, Fay's and Rupert's unrestrained anguish, struggling with the ex- postulations of Lord Grosvenor and Lord Hamp-

ion. Then came a stir without, and two persons entered the smnmer-house, and a sudden hush of surprise fell on all the actors of the little drama. The new-comers were Peggy Willsey and her lover, George Negwyn. The fever of Negwyn had given way before the skillful ministrations of the doctor they had sum- moned on the previous night, and he had been able to continue his journey that morning. On ar- riving at Hamptonwokl, they had been told that the Lady Beatrice was gone to her favourite summer-house on the knoll, and that Lord Tre- velyan was doubtless with her, his lordship being somewhere about the grounds. Anxious to have the interview soon over, Peggy had procured the necessary assistance, and Negwyn made nis ap- pearance, carried between two men. Adlowe recognised the man at once. His face turned to an ashen paleness. He comprehended, from the new, strange look on the face of his late confederate, that he was remorseful and repentant. He slunk back, and tried to make his escape un- perceived. But Negwyn's eye was upon him, and Negwyn's thin finger pointed him out. "Stop him !" he said. "Stop Lord Adlowe I have a confession to make, and he is implicated in it." One of the policemen, at a sign from Lord Tre- velyan, detained the guilty profligate. "My name is George Negwyn, said the valet. " Latay I was in Lord Adlowe's service, under the assumed name of Haskins." A sensation followed this announcement. Most of the persons present were familiar with the name. "Eighteen years ago," continued Negwyn, leaning heavily on his supporters, "I was valet to Lord Adlowe and to Mr. Geoffrey Trevelyan. And this is Mr. Geoffrey ?" he added, fixing his gaze upon the chief prisoner. "Mr. Geoffrey, forgive Inc. I could have cleared you years ago, but that Lord Adlowe hired me to keep out of the way. You are innocent, and I can prove it." A look of almost holy joy appeared on Geoffrey Trevelyan's face, and he drew the half-fainting Lady Beatrice to his breast. "Speak, Negwyn ! " he exclaimed. "The occurrences of that night are all a mystery to me." Adlowe sneered, and Lord Trevelyan looked in. credulous. "Go on," said the latter, waving his hand. "I remember you well, Negwyn. You look very ill now. What is this romantic story you have to tell ? " "My lord," said Negwyn, solemnly, " I have been like to die. Peggy here has talked to me of my duty, and brought me here from the Burnt Downs, it seems, in the very nick of time. Surely God must have put into her head—" "Proceed with your story," interrupted the marquis. The men who had brought Negwyn from the carriage laid him on the bamboo lounge, by Peggy Willsey's directions, and Peggy herself propped hini up so that he could command a view of his audience. "My lord," he said, addressing himself to Lord Trevelyan, and speaking with all the solemnity of truth, "you have been a deceived man all these years. Mr. Geoffrey never did the crime with which you charged him." "But I saw him with my own eyes " cried the marquis, fiercely. Negwyn weut on, not heeding the interrup- tion. "My lord, on that night, eighteen years ago, Mr. Geoffrey Trevelyan and Lord Adlowe were sitting in my lord's chamber, when I entered the ante-room adjoining, unseen, as I thought, by either of my young masters. Lord Adlowe had been brewing a punch, and I saw him turn aside and pour into his cousin's glass some liquid from a small vial, which he brought out from his pocket. I said nothing not thinking the matter very ser- ious, but from that moment I watched my lord. Mr. Geoffrey drank the punch that had been pre- pared for him, all the while protesting against the use of liquor; and when he had finished, Lord Adlowe proposed that they should eat opium for an experiment. The punch seeme& to have gone to Mr. Geoffrey's head, and he assented. He took the opium. Lord Adlowe did not touch it. "So far I remember I" cried. Geoffrey Trevelyan, eagerly. "But then follows a blank. What came next ?" "Then Lord Adlowe went to Mr. Geoffrey's room, and got Mr. Geoffrey's dagger that he kept among his curiosities. Then his lordship led Mr. Geoffrey to the marquis's room, going as still as mice. I followed on tiptoes. My lord went into Lord Trevelyan's chamber, leading Mr. Geoffrey like a child. The marquis was asleep. Lord Ad- lowe bent over him, thrust the dagger Quick into his shoulder with his own hands, put Mr. Geoffrey's hand on the dagger hilt, and rushed out into the, hall just in time to avoid discovery. This is the truth. I swear it I" Adlowe muttered a wild curse. There was a breathless silence. Negwyn re- sumed : " You all know what happened next—the accu- sation of Mr. Geoffrey, and his expulsion from the Park That very night I told Lord Adlowe that I had seen all. He paid me a big sum of money to keep quiet, and gave me my passage to Australia. I have been off there till I came home this spring. I was to get a nice pile of money

when he came into t::e -1 reveiyan property. my Lord Trevelyan, I have told the whole story exactly as it happened. I will give you my oath on it.' The marquis fixed his stern eyes on Negwyn's -Patid-fa.:66. He read only atithfulnees there. Thee he looked at Geoffrey, who met his gaze with those fearless, honest blue eyes he had loved so well. Then, last of all, he looked at Adlowe, and the baffled schemer's gaze fell, and a guilty look over- spread his sinister cor nteuance. The mystery was cleared at last, and Geoffrey Trevelyan was proved to be innecent, noble and heeelirs.ble, as one wenn n's heart had always be- lieved him. " My God !" said the marquis, the whole truth 'rushing upon his soul in a flood of light. "How have I wronged him ! Geothey—" He looked at his wronged nephew, his old love for him shining from every grand and noble feature, and he half held out his hand, withdrawing it quickly. " No," he said, as if to himself, tears flooding his eyes, "it is too late ! I have sinned against him beyond forgiveness! He hates me now I Let me go away to the lonely misery I merit !" He put out his hands, groping his way to the door. • But he had not gained the threshold when a light step hurried after him, and a pair of girlish, cling- ing arms drew him back. It was Giralda's face that his eyes looked on— Gira da, tender, loving, compassionate. • "Dear uncle," she cried, "you must not go I I love you. I have loved you from the first. You will not leave me ?" The marquis looked at her incredulously. He could not believe that she had forgiven him, that she loved him still. It needed the precious confirmation she gave when she stole her arms around his neck, and pressed her soft clicek to his bearded one, and when releasing him, she drew him toward her father, saying simply : " Papa, wont you and uncle be friends again ? He loves you and you love him, and I shall never be happy if he is miserable.' Lord Trevelyan broke down in tears and sobs, blessing Giralita, and Geoffrey met hina half-way in a cordial embrace. Then followed a- scene of wild rejoicing. The marquis embraced the Lady Beatrice and her chil- dren ; and Lord Hampton, prond and happy, followed his example, congratulating Geoffrey on the happy termination of all his troubles. In the midst of all the joy and gladne,s, Lord Aillowe, Watching his opportunity, broke from the, restraining hand of the policeman, darted past the detective, and made his escape. "Let him go," said Lord Trevelyan, looking on the happy group. "He carries his own punish- ment with him." The marquis was a true prophet. Disgraced and poor, Adlowe made haste to quit England : and not many mouths later he perished miserably in a dingy little foreign town, and there was not one to weep for him. • He found a portion at least of his reward in this life. The marriage of the young Grosvenor and Giralda was not long deferred. There is not a hap- pier home in the world than that at the Eagle's Eyrie, not a more devoted and admiring husband, not a sunnier, lovelier young wife! And all goes well with them. At the cottage on the Burnt Down there is a happy, honeA couple, the love and devotion of Peggy having effected a great moral change in Negwyn. Of course, there was a nine days' wonder and gossip among her fashionable friends when the truth came out concerning the Lady Beatrice, and when everybody knew that she had been actually married for many years and had a secret family. But people romance, and the story only gave greater prestige to the beautiful belle, and rendered Geoffrey Trevelyan a lion of the most leonne description. They reside for a good part of the year at Tre- velyan Park which has been repaired and beautified, and is now as fine a place as Hamptonwold. The Flecks, Meggy and Mary, live with them, happy and honoured. The old light has come back to Geoffrey's blue eyes, the old gay smile to his lips. His boys make music in the old house where his childhood was spent, and the old lord of Trevelyan, loved and honoured, clings to them all, and thinks that no man was ever so blessed as he. His last days are, in truth, his best days. And the Hampton Mystery—a puzzle and a mystery no langer—is the glorious centre of all these happy lives.

div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

MY DEAREST NULLIE, Is there ever to be a limit to the width of our sleeves and skirts? Every day they get wider, and from Paris come dresses with a circumference of, seven or eight yards, standing out round the hem. This looks ominously like a return of the dreaded crinoline, and I am convinced that before the summer is over we shall have to stand together If we mean to avoid wearing what nearly everyone is agreed is a hideous and ungraceful costume. Sleeves, as I eaf.d, are wider than ever, and they are stiffened wi h canvas, buckram, or even whale- bone, and altogether the short, plump woman is in evil case this winter, for, unless she is suffi- ciently stron-rninded to fly directly in the face of Dame Fashion, she must resign herself to look her worst until narrower skirts and sleeves of more modest pope: t;or.s come in again.

A somewhat novel production is a saml.fibting jacket of I,rown cloth and plush, which is more comfortable than a tight coat worn over a thick winter gown. The cloth should be more of the Havana or beaver shade, to make a contrast with the plush. Skunk fur, about one and a.half inch wide, is charming on this coat, or brown racoon, mink, or sable may be emploYed. The plastron is simply formed by linos of jer, laid on the cloth, and at the back a triangle of the jit set ia lines trims the basque from the edge to the wtda'. The beck Is very closely shaped, and it is only in front that the coat hsngs loose. The tur trimming may be carried quite to the edge of the ba,que in front, but the pointed style is vary becoming to most figures. Allow three yards of plush, four and a-half yards of for, and two yards cf tifty-inoh cloth.

A great dell of jet or iridesuent sequins is being worn on bonnets. The equine are now set so closely together as to almost resemble the scales of a fish. A bonnet which I saw recently was made somewhat in the Dutch shape, coming down rather long over the ears, and was covered with small eleotrio blue and black sequins, so arranged that their oolours seemed to change with every movement of the wearer. In front, there was a small bunch of violets, and at the bank a rosette and upstanding ends of lint blue and green ribbon, and nestling behind it another bunch of flowers. Another, of rather picturesque detail, was made of terra-cotta felt with a bouillonne of black velvet on the edge of the brim, and the crown trimmed with talveb, a blackbird, and a white paradise plume.

Velvet figures, as I just said, among the fashion. able materials fo- gowns, aud nothing can be prettier than a rioh sapphire blua. A dress of this sort was princess-shaped of the blue velvet, the back fitting the figure and falling in a small troll. The fronts, falling quite loosely, op.n over the front of a delicate seashell-pink silk, which WBB gathered twice at the neck, arui fell in loose straight folds to the feet. Deep-tinted lace was arranged each side in °wade form from just below the waist, and VIM (tarried round the neck so as to form a deep cape over the shoulders and round the beck. The plain collar was of velvet, also the sleeves, which were slashed with strips of pink. Something quite different is a gownsof fancy material in a mixture of dark green splashed with gold. The cape. out up in deep battlements, is new and stylish, and the effect enhanced by trimmings of black satin which appear throughout the dress. Yours lovingly, JENNIE.

div.head: CARLYLE'S lIIPRESSIONS OF THE QUEEN.
div.p: CARLYLE'S lIIPRESSIONS OF THE QUEEN.
"A COMELY LIPTLE- LADY," " POLITE LITTLE
WOMAN."

A letter by Carlyle, written in March, 1869, descrip- tive of his interview with thg Queen at the residence of Dean Stanley, is published in the" At henceum " for the first time. The following passage shows ,the impres- sion made by tier Majesty on the rugged Scotsman The Stanleys and we were in all in a flow of talk, and some flunkeys had done setting coffee pots and tea cups of a sublime pattern, when her Majesty, punctual to the minute, glided in, escorted by her Dame-in- I Waiting (a Duchess Dowager of Athol), and by the Princess. Louise, decidedly a very pretty young lady,and clever too, as I found out in talking to her afterwards. The Queen came softly forward, a kindly little smile on her face, gently shlok hands with all the three women, gently acknowledged with a nod the silent bovks of us male monsters, and directly in her presence everyone was at e,iss again. She is a comely little lady, with a pair of kind, clear, and intelligent grey eyes, still looks almost young (in spire ef one broad wrinkle which . shows on each cheek oce4sionaily), is still plump, has a fine low voice, soft in her whole mariner, is melodiously perfect. It is impossible to imagine a politer little woman ; nothing the least imperious, all gentle, all sincere looking,. unembarrassing, rather attractive, even makes you feel, too (if you have any sense in you), that she is Queen. After a little word to each of us— to me it was, Sorry you did not see my daughter' (Princess of Prussia), or ' all sorry '—perhaps so—which led us to Potsdam, Berlin, St for an instant or two. To Sir Charles Lyell I heard her say, `Gold in Suther- land, but quickly and delicately cut him short in res- ponding. To Brewning, ' Are you writing anything ' (who has just teen publishing the absurdest things) ? ToGrote, I did not heir whit she said, hut it was touch and go with everytridy—majesty visibly without interest, or nearly so, of her own."

CLYMER—" After all, society is a hollow thing ?" Cooley—" You closet seem able to get into it, though." "DID you and Dennis Anderson_ come to terms in your dispute ?" asked a business man of his coachman. Yes, sor ; and very uncompliment'ry terms they wor, sor." MRS. GRIMSHAW -" He was awfully unlucky to break his leg.' Mrs. Malaprop —" I don't see how you can say so. He recovered £l5O damages, and it cost only £2O to have it set." "QUEER critters women is," said Uncle Jehiel. "When one of 'em starts in to git a man all the others tries to head her off, an' then, soon as she gits him, they all turn round and help her to man- age him." Fox a neat mixture of metaphors it is not easy to beat the opening sentence of a recent paragraph in a morning contemporary—" Many are the pit- falls which lie in the path of a man who sits down to make his will."

AN old Scottish matron was one day sadly com- plaining of the depravity of modern times. She wound up her diatribe with the assertion that "Paradise was now changed into a pair o' dice, and matrimony into a matter o' money.' MRS. Yotnio—" I'm afraid my husband is killing himself with overwork." Mrs. Odds—" How is that ?" Mrs. Young " Why, when we first got married he always got home from his office at five, and now he is often kept until ten." Nis. BROWN—" You don't seem to have a very high opinion of your husband's ability ?" Mrs. Malaprop—" No, he's a very ignorant man. Last night he spoke of persdns acting in concert when he should have known that they only sing at such ente,tainments." A SCOTCH boy was one morning at breakfast, when he bawled out, 'Oh, mistress, there's a flea running in the milk, and its legs are touching the bottom." The mistress said, " What, Jock, de ye no' get eneuch o' milk?" The boy replied, "0, yes, mistress, plenty for the porridge I get." AT a dinner party one day, Sir John H--, whose character was considered not to be altogether unexceptionable said he would give them a toast, and looking hard in the face of Mrs. M--, who was more celebrated for wit than beauty, gave "Honest men an' bonny lasses I' " With all my heart, Sir John,' said Mrs. M--, "for it neither applies to you nor me." LITTLE BY.SsIE had been offended in some way. She went off into a corner of the room and turned her back on the company. "I'm mad," she exclaimed, sulkily. "I wish I didn't have any papa or mamma.' "That's wrong, dear," said her mother. "We are the best friends you have.' "Well," said Bessie, still sulking, " I don't mind havin' papa. He isn't here much. But I m gettin' awful iired of the rest of you." Two schoolboys one day, on the banks of the Yarrow, observed a bird's nest built on the arch of a bridge over a deep pool. They were most anxious to get at the eggs, but could think of no way of accomplishing their object. At last it was resolved that one should hold on by the edge of the bridge, and the other creep down and hold by his neighbour's legs. When nearly accomplishing their object the uppermost boy got tired, and called out to his neighbour, " Hold, hold, till I spit on my hands," and with that both of them fell Into the water and were nearly drowned.

"Not at all, sir, replied she; "I only praise the hatter ; had the head or face been worth notice, I should nob have thought of the hat." This is somewhat like the ma- who advertised " Red Children's Stockings—Black Men's Leather Gloves—Plain Ladies' Fur Soles—and Mahogany Children's Chairs WOULDN'T BY. Van Pelt: "There is a line on the front of the card which forbids that." Wool : "That was the only way I could account lor it." STAGE MANAGER (of the Farce Comedy Com- pany) ; " we do? The men have made a mistake and set the stage for the third act instead of the first! Proprietor : "That's all right. Tell 'em to go ahead with the third act, and have the first afterwards. Nobody will know the difference !"

Note; port of the proceedings has been published, 1)0 agreement has been found, and recommendation: favouring union will be submitted to the nei annual meeting of both bodies.

div.head: MINUTES.
div.p: THE MINUTES.

The MAYOR moved the -a-LiTai-o-;; of the minutes of the previous meetings whereupon Councillor Davies called attention to the fact that Councillor Woods was recorded as being on both sides in the division with regard to the Old Barracks,at the previous meeting.—lt was however, explained that this was a decided mistake, Councillor Woods' name having been substituted for that of Coun- cillor Wilkinson in one instance.

div.head: MISTIMED INQUIRY,
div.p: A MISTIMED INQUIRY,

The MAYOR having moved the adoption of the minutes of the Watch Committee. Councillor SMETHURST asked if no communication had been received from respectable ratepayers and shopkeepers, and if so, should it not Ise read to the Council. The MAYOR said he did not know anything about it. Councillor SMETHURST : There has been a letter sent by a certain body. The TOWN CLERK : What does the letter refer to; let us know from whorft it comes. Councillor SMETHURST : From the Ratepayers' Asso- ciation. The MAYOR: That does not arise on these minut4es at all. _

The minutes were then confirmed. THE APPOINTMENT OF ASSISTANT OVERSEERS, &C. The Finance and Estate Committee recommended that an application be made to the Local Government Board for an order pursuant to sections 33 and 34 of the Local Government Act, 1894, to confer on the Council the following matters, viz., (a) The revocation of appoint- ment of assistant overseers; (b) The powers, duties or liabilities of overseers; (e) The powers of a vestry under the 3id and 4th sections of the Poorßate Assessment and Collection Act, 1869; (d) All the powers, duties, and liabilities of a Parish Council under sections 5,6, 10 and 14 of the Act. Councillor SHAW-GREEN moved the adoption of the minutes, and the MAYOR seconded. Councillor DAVIES objected to the form of the applica- tion to be made to the Local Government Board, and after some discussion it was decided to alter the first clause so as to include the " appointment " as well as the "revocation of appointment "of assistant overseers. The minutes were then passed. HEALTH COMMITTEE.

Alderman RIITT;;FiI-MOW--th—e- adoption of the minutes, said that the Council would notice that there was a resolution recommending the General Purposes Committee to present a petition against the Liverpool New Cattle Market Bill. In that bill, powers were sought to provide markets and slaughter-houses within the Hundred of West Derby, which included War- rington. It was that which they objected to in the bill. Councillor ROBERTS seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. A NEW LONGFORD SCHEME.—NOYEL WAY OF EXHIBITING

, the Council at all, but it had been the policy of the cons- mittee for a long time, and he hoped it would continue to he their policy, to submit the whole of their business of public interest to the Council. The committee had not come before the Council with a divided opinion on the matter : they were unanimous that Mr. Madelev merited an advance of salary. He had been a servant of the Corporation for 20 years. When appointed the population of the borough was only 36,000, now it was 57,000. A great increase had incurred in the work of the Museum. The books in the library for which Mr. Madeley was responsible, in the year 1874 only num. , bored 11,000 ; to-day there were 30,000. The library ha been made free, and there were 21,000 books in circula- tion instead of 18,000 as used to be the case, and that I spoke volumes for the interest the public took in the in- stitution. Mr. Madeley possessed great ability and in- telligence that few men in his position possessed, and , although he was not a specialist upon any particular sub- ject, there was hardly a single subject in connection with the Museum upon which he did not possess re- markable information. He was also secretary to the Technical Institute. There were 900 scholars and 75 classes. The season began in September, and did not end till June. His work began at 9.30 in the morning and frequently did not cease till ten o'clock at night. The proposed increase would in no sense become a charge on the rates. This was the only committee which was limited in its expenditure to the amount of its income. Councillor GREENING seconded the motion. Councillor Dams asked what was Mr. Madeley's present salary. Alderman SorroN said that it was £220 a year. Councillor limas : Would not that amount to £3OO, with house, coal, gas, rates, and taxes.

Alderman WRIGHT': Yes.' Councillor DevrEs then asked whether the Town Clerk had not received a communication from some one on the matter. The TOWN CLERK replied that he had from a resident of Little Sankey, which he had shown to the chairmen ef the committee. Councillor SHAW If the Town Clerk is in possession of any letter from any one outside the Council it ought to be read to the Council. The Towsr CLERK said that it was only from a gentle- man objecting to the increase. He was not a ratepayer of the borough. Councillor SHAW contended that although he might not be a ratepayer at present, Little Sankey was likely to come with the borough within a short time. Councillor HEATON and Counciller WOODS supported the proposed increase. Councillor SMETHURST strongly opposed the pro- posed increase, although he had nothing to say against Mr. Madeley's abilities, and alluded to the large num- ber of empty houses in Warrington at the present moment. Mr.Madeley's present salary was £220 a year, and yet it was proposed to give him another £3O. Councillor Smethurst then proceeded to refer to the salary given to a librarian in another town, which had a population of 119,000, and who had 82,833 books to look after, yet his salary only amounted to £lBO a year with house, gas, and C9al. Councillor GREENING spoke in favour of the proposed increase, and contrasted the present condition of the Museum with its position 21 years ago. The Warrington Museum had been put in the Arst class of Museums. Councillor SHAW rose to speak, but The MAYOR said that he could then ask a question,but must not make a speech. Councillor SHAW continued to make some observations in the form of a speech, when the Mayor ruled him out of order. Councillor Slaw still persisted,when the MAYOR again exclaimed warmly : You are out of order, and I won't

listen to you. Councillor Sassy said that he would now proceed with his question. In many towns in England where tech- nical education was being promoted they bad within the precincts of the building a laboratory for the elemen- tary department. The MAYOR (very warmly) : I will not listen to you. You are out of order, and I say you have t sit down. You are out of order.

Councillor Shaw then resumed his seat. Councillor Rommvs,in reply to the various speakers, said he did notsay there would be no charge on the rates. The whole establishment was a charge on the rates. What he said was that this would not be an ad- ditional charge on the rates because the expenditure of the establishment was absolutely limited to a certain amount. The bulk of the gentlemen present could see the difference between this and an additional burden upon the rates. Councillor SMETHURST : That won't do. Councillor ROBERTS: I cannot help your obtuseness. I was not responsible for your brains. Councillor SmErnonsv (to Councillor-Roberts) : You have no right to use such remarks. I suppose I have as good brains as you. The minutes were then agreed to, Councillor Smet- hurst being the only dissentient. CEMETERY COMMITTEE: THE MICE OF CLERK. The committee passed a resolution to the effect that the duties of the Registrar will not permit of his officiating as clerk at any funeral in future. Councillor HILL, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said the committee thought there was quite sufficient work for the registrar to do without attending to the duties of other people. Councillor Sifirzcocx seconded the motion, and it was carried.

div.head: PLANS.
div.p: PLANS.

Councillor MONKS in -M-O-Virng the adoption of the minutes of the Sanitary Works Committee said that there was an application for permission ;or further expenditure for Longford Works. At one time, even in his short recollection as a member of the Council, a pro- posal such as that to spend Rloney for the further ex- tension of Longford, would have aroused such a spirit of opposition as he felt sure would have totally prevented a calm and quiet discussion of such a proposal. The question had been well discussed and considered by the sub-committee and the general con.mittee. There had been considerable difference of opinion amongst the members as to what was the right thing to do. At the end of twelve months' working,therefore, they had been able to incorporate all that was best and to leave out all that was disadvantageous. If any member of the Council had any suggestions to make that evening relative to the matter, he was sure that the committee would gladly consider them, brit if not they, on the other hand, hoped that the Council would accept their recommendation unanimously. The resolution was brought forward now because the matter was one of urgent necessity. He thought the scheme they had pro- pared was the best they could have. It had been brought about by the breaking of a boiler, which had been work- , ing night and day for the last ten or eleven years, and with material having a corrosive action upon the plates. The boiler had been also in the charge of men who could not be called experienced. They were little better than labourers, in fact, and had been employed instead of iremen in order to practise economy. The boiler had been condemned, and the repairs necessary would cost £375, whereas they could obtain a new boiler for £4BO, which included the cost of putting it in its proper posi- tion. To put a new boiler down would also occupy less time than would be exhausted in repairing the old one. The committee had thought that it would be better to go in for a new boiler, and had deemed it desirable that ,it should be placed in a different position. At this stage, Councillor Monks had a number of plans thrown by limelight upon a screen which was placed upon a wall of the Council Chamber, and in a very lucid manner, he explained the proposed altera- tions. Proceeding, Councillor Maxis remarked that they had sufficient orders on their books for the sale of all the manure which would be manufactured during the next twelve months. That was a very satisfactory state of things. (Hear, hear.) Last year 584 tons of dried manure were sold, and the stock was cleared out except five tons. They would make a few tons more this year than they did the year before. They were going on satisfactorily, and the returns as presented to the com- mittee every fortnight were also satisfactory. They felt that the depst was a credit not only to the committee but to the Corporation as a whole. He had every con- fidence in submitting the minutes, and he hoped the Council would confirm the motion he had made. (Ap- plause. Councillor BEAMAN seconded the minutes. Alderman SUTTON expressed his indebtedness to Coun- cillor Monks: for his able and lucid statement. Be should like to know what the scheme would ccst when completed. Would it not be better to defer doing any piecemeal work and have one good job at the Longford Depot? Counoillor SITAW Gems also congratulated Councillor Monks upon his able speech, but suggested that the whole scheme should be complete so that it might be presented to the Local Government Board, and they would be able to see how far they were likely to be led ' into expenditure. Alderman BOLTON would support the provision of a , new boiler,as he thought it was better to have A new one at £4BO than spend £375 in the repair of an old one. Councillor R. .T. FAIRCLOUGH said he had been over the works and he thought the alterations which were being made were a step in the right direction. Councillor Monis, in reply, said he could not at pre- sent give an opinion as to the total cast of the scheme. He pointed out that it was intended to provide accom- modation for the men in which to wash themselves, as they had dirty work to do. They did not intend to pro- vide elegant bath rooms with brass fittings and hot and sold water taps and shower bath. Brick and tile places would be provided,which would he suitable for the men. Better vans should be provided for rase in the street, as they had been in use for a great number of years. With regard to the expenditure, the Committee were limiting themselves to £1,500, and not another halfpenny would be spent until the Council had an opportunity of con- sidering the whole scheme. They did not want to go in for the whole scheme at once, They wished to make the extension piecemeal—over three or four years' time— and not to do the work as it were to morrow. The minutes were then agreed to. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE : MORE WOOD PAVEMENTS. Alderman WRIGHT, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, observed that the committee had made a re- port upon the worst streets and passages in the town, and these would be dealt with during the present year. They expected to attend to 100 such streets and pas- sages. With regard to the proposed wood pavement in Springfield-street, the owners of the adjoining property were paying the additional cost between the setts and wood pavement. They were getting no special advan- tage without paying for it. Councillor HEATON seconded the passing of the minutes. GOIITICiIIOT GREENING expressed a hope that that part of Museum-street near the Lecture-rnom would also be paved with wood, as it would be a great comfort and convenience ti those attending lectures. Alderman WRIGHT said that the matter had already been brought under his notice, and he could promise that the matter should have the consideration of the committee. The minutes were eonfirmed. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. OAS COMMITTER.

At a meeting of the Gas Committee, held on the 25th January, if was resolved that the tender of Mr. Edward Wood to supply and fix at Longford, columns and girders for coal stores and purifier house at £BB7 be accepted. Councillor R. T. Fartictouart,in moving the confirma- tion of the Gas Committee's minutes, said he wished to withdraw the resolution with respect to the tender of Mr. Edward Wood. Councillor FIESTON seconded the proposition. Councillor BEAMAN wished to know Councillor Fair. dough's reasons for withdrawing the resolution. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH answered that it would net be in the interests of the retepayers to give the reasons. The minutes were then accepted. RIVERS' commrTTIM.

Councillor ROBERTS, in proposing the minutes of this committee which appeared in our last issue, said that the result of the conference recently held was that the Town Clerk had drawn up a new series of proposals which they 'proposed to submit te the Ship Canal Com- pany in a few days. When they received a reply from the company there would be a further conference upon the matter. Councillor HEATow seconded, and the minutes were passed. WATER COMMITTEE.—TRE RESIGNATION OF MR. ROSS. Alderman FRANCOMB moved the confirmation of the minutes which appeared in our last issue. He said that the committee wished to withdraw the resolution with regard to Mr. Ross. It was proposed that that gentle- man should leave them on the Ist July, but he had since taken another course, and they would have him with them until the sth November. That was why he (the speaker) wished to w;thdraw the resolution. Councillor STIAW GREEN seconded. Councillor DAVIES suggested that the latter part of the resolution which referred to the application for a suc- cessor shouts] be oontinued. Alderman FRANCOMB, in rep'v, said he had the same feeling at one time, and even at the present time he I looked forward to haViIIT a new man with them for two or three months before I,tr. Ross left. div.head: FORTUNES BY ACCIDENT.
div.p: FORTUNES BY ACCIDENT.

The old proverb, " Accidents will happen in the best ' regulated families," acquires a new force when we see on every hand that an accident erten gives to the in- ventor fame and fortune. Edison's discovery of the phonograph was the result of an accident, although the eminent Plectrician avers that this lucky accident is the only one from which, during his career as an inventor, he has derived benefit. _ It was an accident, too, which led to the discovery of the means by which a number of lines in the construc- tion of a house ensure the greatest safety to the build- ing. Mr. McLaughland, the mathematician, had been I engaged upon the solution of the problem for many years. Ile had almost given up his efforts to achieve a solution when one day he accidently looked at the cell of a honey bee. Much interested in its construction, he. carefully examined it. The result of that examination gave him the key to the whole position—the solution of the problem. The odd side of the discovery lies in the fact that this problem had puzz'ed the heads of three centuries of mathematicians. Lovers of snuff are doubtless aware that the famous " Lundyfnot " snuff was discovered by accident A fire at a Dublin snuff-maker's, instead of bringing ruin, gave the manufacturer an idea. Whilst viewing the ruins of his house of busines the snuff-maker mechani- cally p:cked up a box of burnt snuff. From force of habit he lifted it to his nose. Its flavour startled him— he had discevereci a new kind which would throw all others in the shade. In a few ysars he had made a fortune. Millionaires are already familiar with the accident Nvhich give a tobicconlst the idea of wrapping tobacco in tinfoil, and the forther accident which enabled a workman to roll the tinfoil sufficiently thin to make its usa profitable. The discovery of lithography was the retilt of an accident. In the year 1796. we are told, the citizens of Munich had just vritnessed the first triumphant perform- ance of zart's opera, " Don Juan," and the theatre was deserted by all save one man,Alois Sennefelder,who,

, after making a round of inspection irt t he building to see that no sparks had ignited anything comoustible,retired to his room to stamp the tieketa of admission for the following day. When he entervd his apartment he had three things in hie hands—a poliched whetstone who*, he had purchased for snarpening ran ire, a ticket stamp still moistened with printing ink, and a cheque on the treasurer of the theatre for his weekly salary. As he placed the cheque upon the table, a gust of wind swept it high up in his room for a moment, and then deposited it ia a basin filled with water. Sennefelder dried the wet paper as well as he could, and then weighed it down with the whetstone,upon which he had carelessly placed the printing stamp. When he returned to his room the following morning he was astonished at seeing the letters of the stamp printed with remarkable accuracy upon the dampened paper. A thought came to him. He wondered whether, by some such means, ha could not simplify his work of continually copying the songs of the chorus. He went out and purchased a large stone, commenced making experiments, and, as we all 'now now, finally discovered the art of printing from stone— lithography. The hints of the telephone were rectived by accident, in an instant almost, by Bell. Ericsson received the hint of the screw propeller whilst idly watching a fish swimming in a quiet pool; and an accident—a railway accident—gave Westinehouee the first suggestion of the air brake. His train was brought to a standstill and the guard told him a collision had °warred. Then it occurred to him that it should be possible to invent some mechanical appliance which would give an engineer command of a train such as he did not possess in the use of the throttle and the reversing lever. He turned over this idea in his mind, and being skilful with his hands and having the capacity of the inventor, he constructed in a little while the first model of the air brak3 It happened that not long afterwards he wee in . • Chicago, and he met an inventor who thought that to him had come the inspiration for the perfect brake, and had such faith in this inspiration that he worked it out, and had secured patents for his design. "I, too," said Westinghouse, " have a scheme for a railway brake , which will enable the driver of a train to apply the brake from the engine to the last carriage, and will ' bring a train to a standstill in far less time than the hand-brake now in use can do." " Ah, but," the older inventor said, " you cannot make a brake which will do these things without infringing upon my patents. " I can and will," replied young Westinghouse ; and within a year he had done his work sad found himself to be a famous man.
tietstone whi.•h

It was a curious accident which led to the discovery of the principle of manufacturing satin. A silk weaver, in despair at not selling his material, unconsciously put several threads in his mouth. When he spat them out, he was astonished at their glossy appearance. This accident gave him the idea of producing a new material, to which was given the name of "satin." Dr. Gatling's accidental presence at a battle gave him the idea for his famous Gatling gun. "In 1861," he says, "I was living in Indianapolis. My residence was near the depot, and I often saw troops of volunteers leaving for the front, or when the dead bodies were brought home for burial. The sight of these poor men at once gave me the idea of inventing some deadly gun which would shorten warfare and lessen suffering."

When the idea of the telegraph was first accidentally suggested to Morse, he was a popular and successful Painter, yet he abandoned his art,and for years endured the greatest hardship in order to develop and perfect the idea which had coma to him. "Indeed, so straightened were my circumstances," be wrote after- wards, " that in order to save time to carry out my in- vention and to economise my scanty means, I for many maths lodged and ate in my studio, procuring my food in small quantities from some grocery, and preparing it myself. To conceal from my friends the stinted manner in which I lived, I was in the habit of bringing my food to my rooms in the evenings, and this was my mode of life for many years."

WHAT DREAMS MAT COME. Is a recent lecture at the Royal Institution, Dr. B. W. Richardson says that the sleep of health is dreamless. " Dreams " says Shakespeare "are children of an idle brain." If both the doctor aril poet are right it follows that idle brains are unhealthy brains. N o doubt there might be truth In the inference, but that is not quite the point. Are all dreams signs of a deceased condition To this the doctor says "No." Be divides dreams into two classes ; those started by noises or other causes outside the sleeper, and those produced by pain, fever, or indigestion.

Here we inject a fact. We recei re multitudes of letters containing this affirmation, almost in identical word. : /seas worse tired in the worni ug than when I tun, to led." To this the dector ha an answer. He says. " flh en we feel teearied in the Inoreauveery likely it results front dreams that lee have forgotten." Quite so.

In other words there is a bodily condition which may prevent a person from working by day at his usual calling, but obliges him to labour at night under a mental stimulus of which he knows nothing save by its resulting exhaustion. These unhappy wretches toil harder, therefore, for no compensation, when they ate ill, than they have to do to earn a living when they are well. What an infernal and frightful fact ! And this too without taking into account their 'physical suffering at all times. " Night," said Coleridge, "Is my hell."

From one of the letters referred to we quote what a woman says of her daughter : " she was worse tired in a morning Man when she went to bod." Poor girl. Those" forgotton dreams" had tossed her about as a ship is tossed in the tempest. Night was her day of labour.

The mother's simple tale is this: 'ln June, 1890, my daughter Ann Elizabeth became low, weak, and fretful, and complained of pain in the chest after eating. Next her stomach was so irritable that she vomited all the food she took. It was awful to see her heave and strain. ?or three weeks nothing passed through her stomach except a little soda water and lime water' Later en, her feet and legs began to swell and puff from dropsy, She was now as pale as death and looked as though she had noc a drop of blood in her body, and was alwaya cold. Month after month dragged by an she got weaker every day. She could not walk withone a support, for she had lost the proper use of her legs, and her body swayed from side to side as she moved. "A doctor attended her for twelve months,and flnal'y sald it was use giving her any more medicine as it I would de her no good. In May, 1891, I took her to the Dewehury Infirmary. She got no better there, and I thought I was surely going to lose her. She was then thirteen years of age. " One day a lady (Mrs. Lightoller) called at ley shop, and seeing how bad my daughter was, spoke of a medi- cine called Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and per- suaded us to try it. I got a bottle from the Thornhill Lees Co-operative Stores, and she began taking it. In two days she found a little relief ; the sickness was not so frequent. She kept on with the Syrup and steadily Improved. She soon was strong as ever, and has since been in the best of health and can take an kind of food. After she had taken the Syrup only two weeks the neighbours were surprised at her improved appearance and I told them what had brought it about—that Seigel's Syrup had done what the doctors could not do, it sawed her life. Yours truly (Signed), (Mrs.) Sanaa ANN SHEARD, 19, Brewery -lane, Thornhill Lees, near Dewsbury, October 11th, 1892."

The inciting cause of all this young girl's pitiful suffer ing was indigestion and dyspepsia, dropsy being one of. its most dangerous symptoms. It attacks both youth and age, its fearful and otten fatal results bemg due to the fact that physicians usually treat the symptoms in stead of the 'disease.

" A child's dreams," says Dr. Richardson. " are signs of disturbed health and shculd be regard ed with anxiety." The same is true of the dreams of older people. They can poison in the stomach and point to the immediate so of M3ther Seigel's Curative Syrup.

BARBER: How would you like to have your hair eats sir?" Customer: "With scissors, sir! Did ye s'pose I wanted it done with a scythe?" AN EXAMINATION AT A SCHOOL BOARD.— Inspector: "In which of his battles was Gustavus Adolphus killed ?" Pupil: "I think it was in his last." THERE is a hairdresser in a suburban district who has hit on a new idea. He tells his customers such horrible stories that it makes their hair stand on end. It is so much easier for him to cut it then, he says. "Six feet in his boots! " exclaimed old Mrs. Flatiron. "Nonsense! Why, they might as well tell me that the man has six heads in his hat !" JACK TAR: "We ain't so very fur from land, Jim! There's been a yacht along here lately." Jim: "How do you know?" Jack Tar: "See all them champagne corks." THE HUSBAND'S LAMENT.—After a conjugal scene, the wife gave her husband a slap in the face. Instead of flying into a passion the husband very composedly took up his hat, and, before going away, spoke as follows :—" Madame, six years ago, when I solicited your parents for your hand, I little suspected the use you would make of it." "HE referred me to you as to his honesty." "And I certainly can endorse him thoroughly. Why, my dear sir, I'd trust that man with—with an umbrella. LADY COMMERCIAL (to her husband, who is rather cold to her) : "John, the kisses you give me now are not up to the sample you gave me when you asked me to be yours. It isn't busi- ness ! " I SAY, pa, heard the news!" "No, my boy What is it 1" "Why, they aren't going to have the lamp-posts any ionger." "I am surprised. What is the reason!" "Why, they re long enough." EXPECTING Too Ml:TH.—Husband "Here's a bill for a ball costume; what does it mean?" Wife: "Ah ! you know that green robe I wore at the ball at which I was introduced to you last year 1" Husband: " S-o-h ! And you mean to say that I am to pay for the trap in which I was caught?" A MAN went home the other night and found the house locked up. After infinite trouble he managed to gain entrance through a back window, and then discovered on the parlour table a note from his wife, reading, "I have gone out. You will find the key on the side of the step." Nov IMPORTANCE ENOUGH. —" There's one thing," he remarked, factiously, as the tax assessor finished enumerating the various items on the list, "that I never tax." What is that?" asked the assessor. "My brain," laughed the funny man. "Oh well," replied the tax assessor, as he took a good look at him, "there are a lot of little things we never ask about." A MAN who married a widow has invented a device to cure her of "eternally praising" her former husband. Whenever she begins to descant on his noble qualities, this ingenious number two merely says, "Poor dear man! How I wish he had not died!" and the lady immediately begins to think of something else to talk about. BROWNLEIGH (visiting friends in the country): cleri't often get such a good supper." Johnnie:

"Neither do we." "My dear," said a lady to a friend who was complaining of a servant, "you can't expect all the virtues for six shillings a week." "But I pay seven-and-six I" was the practical response. Do you think, young man, that you could give my daughter all she asks for ?" questioned papa, grimly. "I--aw—think so, sir, " murmered the lover, bashfully. "She says she wants only me." FROIE the Hopeful Young Man to the Pastor: "As I stand in the broad avenue of life I find so many closed doors I know not which one to open. How can I tell which will lead me to success ? " From the Practical Pastor to the Young Man: "There's only one, and you'll find it/ labelled 'Push.'" "AND who is this?" asked Aunt Clara, point- ing to the picture of a chubby child in skirts. "That," said Robby, who had been wearing knickerbockers for some time, "is me when I was a girl." FRENCHWOMAN (travelling for first time on Metropolitan Railway, to fellow-passenger) : "My station do seem very long to arrive at. I have passed Bovreel, Asbestos, Liebig, Pears, and Bouillon Fleet, but I come not to the Adeeson Road." MISTRESS: "Good gracious, Susan, the house is on fire!" Susan (an overworked " general ") : Well mum, it's comfortin' to think that at last there's a fire in the 'ouse I 'aven't 'ad to light!" OF COURSE THEY WlLL.—Maude: "What shall we do if those horrid hoop-skirts really become fashionable again?" Mamie: "I suppose we shall wonder how we ever could have worn those horrid skimpy dresses."' OLD LADY: "My doctor recommends me a six months' sea voyage, but I have my doubts about his motives." The Captain: "Why?" Old Lady: "Because my doctor is my son-in-law ! " JUST WIIAT HE WANTED.—HuSbancI (aftEr a sharp quarrel): "You may buy the dress if you like, but I shan't pay for it.' Wife "Then they'll sue you for the amount!" Husband : "So much the better; in that case I'll pawn the piano for the money." ONE night we were sitting out of doors in the moonlight, unusually silent—almost sad. Suddenly someone—a poetic-looking man, with a gentle, lovely face—said, in a low tone :—" Did you ever think of the beautiful lesson the stars teach us?" We gave a vague, appreciative murmur, but some soulless clod said :—" No ; what is it?" "How to wink," he answered, in a sad, sweet voice. IT is customary for members of the House of Commons, when rising to address the House, to commence "Mr. Speaker, sir." One young mem- ber, who was rather nervous, began as follows: "Mr. Speaker, dear sir." "AND so, on reflection, Mr. Fastboy, I have determined that it is best to terminate our engage- ment." "But, Clara, Clara !" exclaimed the heart-broken man, wringing his hands, "won't you wait until I -can find a substitute?" GIRL (on seeing a Chinaman) : What's that, mamma?" Mother: "That a Chinaman, dear." Girl : "Do all the people in China dress like that ?" Mother: "Yes, dear.' Girl: "Gracious 1 How they must laugh when they see each other." "BUT, your honour," said the prisoner, "I am not gui,ty of this crime. I have three witnesses who wilt swear that at the hour this man was robbed I was at home in my own chamber taking care of the baby." "Yes, your honour," glibly answered the prisoner's counsel, "that is strictly true. We can prove a lullaby, your honour." MONEYBAGS: "How did your banquet go off. Banklurk : "Not as well as it might, you know, The toastmaster called on a gentleman who had lost an arm and a leg to answer to the toast 'Our absent members.'" AT Derby station the other day a thin lath of a man was observed to try his weight on the auto- matic machine. The hands retused to budge. What did he do? Did he write a letter threaten- ing the company with an action? No! He simply crept through the slit and regained his "penny.' "ARE these mackerel quite fresh?" asked a lady of a ravged but pompous old fishmonger who came to her door. "Oh, yes, puffickly so, puffiekly so!" was the reply. " Jess nostrilise them and see," " Nostrilise them? What do you mean by that ? " " Why, lady," said the fish purveyor, with a look indicative of, pity for her ignorance, "smell 'em! smell 'em !" A MAN may stop a horse that's tearing down the street, may stop an enemy's advance amid the battle's heat; In fact, stop- almost anything in situations trying; but not a single man alive can stop a baby crying. "TICKETS, PLEASE ! "—A ticket-collector on one of our largest railways is much struck with the enormous mortality which seems to take place" among children at one particular age. Most of them seem to enjoy robust health up to within a few months of their twelfth year, but hardly any, ib would appear, ac,u.dly reach that age. AN EAR FOR MUSIC. Mistress (angrily) : " Bridget! What do you mean by listening out- side the door ?" Bridget : "Shur, mum, oi can't help slitoppiii to lision when oi hear yer beauti- ful voice ; it's bike music, especially them high 110%es whin ye're blowin' up the master I"
