div.head: AN INSURANCE SOCIETY AND ITS
div.p: AN INSURANCE SOCIETY AND ITS
AGENT.
IMPORTANT CASE AT THE COUNTY COURT.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday,last week before his Honour Judge Wynne Foulkes, the Loudon, Edinburgh, and Glasgow Insurance Company,sued John Martin Dale,Friars' Gate, formerly an agent of the Com- pany, for £24 17s. 7d., trade up as follows : cash col- lected by the defendant for the Company and un- I accounted for,the sums of 19s. sd. and £1 95,; unearned special salary paid to the defendant, £2 is. 5d.; and dis- crepancies, 7s. 9d. In addition there was also a claim of £2O for the liquidation of damages on the breach of agreement made between the defendant and the Com- pany, in consequence of which defendant had agreed that within six months after the termination of his en- gagement with the Company, he would not call upon, or canvas the policy holders of the Company,as agent for another insurance company, and endeavour to persuade them to leave the Company. The Company also claimed an injunction against the defendant rest, aining him from acting as agent to any society until the expiration of six months. There was also a claim against Jonathan Hewitson, Bilston, Wolverhampton, for the same sum,as a guarantee. A counter-claim was made against the Company for £4B ss. 9d. by Mr. Dale, made up of sums of £5, and £3 ss. 9d., being monies overpaid by him to the plaintiff, or wrongfully charged by them, and £4O for wrongful dismissal, and the price of the policy book. The Company were repressented by Mr. Rhodes, barrister of Manchester instructed by Mr. Percy Marsh, of Messrs. Richardson and Marsh, Bolton, and the de- ferdant by Mr. Foley, of Bolton. Mr. Rhodes said that Dale entered the service of the Company in September 1893. He signed the usual agreement upon Joining the Society. All went on well until October 23, 1894, when on sending in his usual accounts, there was a deficiency of 1.35. sd. This was sent to the head office in London. On October 28, the defendant wrote a letter to the manager, Thomas Yield, saying that he was sorry that he had sent the accounts short that week, but so many had lapsed. He hoped, however, that with the improvement of trade, he would soon be all right. The officials at the head office, how- ever, instructed the superintendent to send someone round with Dale the next week. Mr. Seddon went round with him on October 30, and there was again a deficiency of £1 9s. upon the accounts which ought to have been paid. He also told Mr. Seddon that he was not in a position to pay to the insurance Company the money upon the accounts. On October 31, Mr. Dale sent in his resignation, but on the following week he was dismissed by the Company. Besides the above mentioned sums there was unearned special salary of £2 Is. sd. It was the custom that when an agent took out new policies, he was advanced six weeks' commission and was then bound to pay back eight weeks' premium. Dalethad entered a considerable number upon his books-32, in fact—but they were not bonafide policies, and defendant had not repaid all the premiums advanced upon them. They therefore claimed the amount which had not been repaid. The next claim was £2O which was under clause 10 of the agreement, which stated that no agent should collect from any other Company within six months after leaving the Company, nor shall canvas on behalf of such Company. If this should be done, a sum of £2O could be claimed for the liquidation of such dam- ages. Immediately after leaving the London, Edinburgh and Glasgow Company, the defendant entered the service of the Refuge Insurance Company, canvassed the persons insured in the London, Edinburgh and Glasgow Insurance Company, on behalf of the Refuge, and told them that the Company was on the point cf breaking, and made many other such statements. He, therefore, submitted that clause 10 had been broken, and that the defendant was liable to pay £2O. The claim against Hewitson was as guarantor.—His Honour said that the guarantor could not be sued along with, the principal.—Mr. Rhodes, however, begged to differ' with his Honour.—The Judge said that if an authority could be found, he would allow it—Mr. Rhodes having shown an authority, his Honour allowed it, and Mr. Rhodes proceeding said that he could not understand how the defendant made out his claim for £5, and £3 ss. 9d!, for moneys over-paid to him to the rlaintiffs, as they had not any account of such money over-paid. With regard to the £4O damages for wrongful dismissal, or in the alternative the right to nominate a successor, the book was the property of the Company, and Mr. Dale had not paid anything for it, therefore, he had no right to nominate a successor. James Seddon, the Superintendent for the Warrington district, said that he engaged the defendant in Septem- ber, 1893. Until August, 1894, he sent in his weekly returns all right. They then began to come in with cash short. Witness lent him the money to square his ac- counts:and the returns wrre then sent right, to the offices of the Company. It was not until Oct. 23. that the returns were sent to the head office short. After de- fendant's dismissal, witness called at one of the policy holders named Thomas, and while there, defendant called, and asked Mrs. Thomas to join the Refuge. Wit ness asked him why he was tampering with the business to which he replied that he had a right to do.—Cross- examined by Mr. Foley : It was not his duty to inspect the policy holders. When he first ran short lin his accounts, wit- ness premised to try to find a customer for his book. He advertised for a customer. The usual price of a book *as between seven and ten times the collectible pre- nium. Witness believed that the reason defendant was discharged was that lie had not carried out the terms of his engagemEnt. Robert Dexter,manager of the Liverpool district for the London, etc., Company, said that became to see Dale to serve him his dismissal. He told Mr. Dale that if he was prepared to pay the cash for the last two weeks' collections, he would use his influence to keep him in the Company's service. Dale replied that he was not in a position to pay. Samuel Wright, J.P., said that he was a collector for the plaintiffs ; and had the book of Dale. He had not paid anything for the book to the Company or anyone else. He met Dale at the ti6use of a Airs. Shepherd, one of the policy-holders, and he was endeavouring to per- suade Mrs. Shepherd to join the " Refuge." Mrs. Shep- herd had not paid to the society since. Witness met Dale in Irlam-st, subsequently, and Dale asked him whether he had bought the book, but witness refused to tell him. The defendant then went on to say that he would do all he could to induce the policy-holders to enter the Refuge Assurance Company. Witness re- minded him of his agreement with the London, &c., Society. He said that he did not care for that, and would fight the business. Catherine Smith, 50, Dallarn-lane, said that Dale had called upon her to join the Refuge, as the other Society was not a good club. Hannah Smith, Lythgoe's-lane, said that Dale called upon her and said that the London, &c., Society had bruken,and produced a paper in proof of this statement. As she could not read, he read extracts from the paper. Further similar evidence was Oven by David Burgess Latchford ; Mary Sharpe, 98, Ilardy-st. ; Mrs. Chester 7, Bayhorse-yard ;and J. W. Doclirey, Ellesmere-st. Mr. Foley then addressed the court for the defence. lie contended that the items of 19s. sd. and £1 95., which were claimed, were moneys which had not been collected by the defendant, and that, therefore, the Company could not claim for them. As to the special salary, the Company had no right to claim eight weeks' premiums unless the defendant had collected that amount. The Company had only the right to claim the amount which the defendant had collected. He also contended that the Company had no right to claim £2O for the breach of agreement. He did not deny that Dale had canvassed some of the policy-holders, but the amount to be claimed from him in consequence must be in proportion to the amount of damages swtained by the Company. The reason that the defendant had failed to pay the sums of 19s. sd. and £1 9s.was the bad trade which had caused so many lapses in policies. Dale wrote to the Company explaining ~this, and on receiving no reply,he sent in his resignation. As soon as his resigna- tion was sent in; the Company dismissed him, and he (Mr. Foley) contended that it was in order to deprive him of his right to get £4O for his book, and his right to nominate his successor. His Honour (interrupting) said that he took it that the right to nominate a successor was suisject to thin approval of the Company. A long argument then ensued between his Honour and Mr. Foley, with respect to thin right of the Company to dismiss the defendant without due notice. His Honour held that the Company were the judges as to whether the collector was attending properly to his duties, while on the other hand. Mr. Foley held that the defendant must have committed some wrong before he could be discharged without notice. John Martin Dale was then called, and after giving cridence for a short time, the case was adjourned, the learned counsel on either side to agree upon the data for re-opening.

div.head: LATE MRS. WICE-CHNIB, OF ..FT. HELENS.
div.p: THE LATE MRS. WICE-CHNIB, OF ..FT. HELENS.

The remains of Mrs. Wliechnie. wife of Alderman D. Mliechnie, an ex-Mayor of St. Helens, of Eccles- ton Grange,were interred in the family vault in the Nonconformist portion of St. Helens Cemetery, on Saturday afternoon. The deceased lady expired at Bournemouth, on Tuesday last,under circumstances previously reported, and the remains were removed to St. Helens on Thursday. The body was enclosed in a polished oak coffin, and the following inscrip- tion appeared on a brass shield:—" Agnes ltf•Rechnie, died January 28th, 1895, aged 59 years." The Rev. J. Brown, pastor of the Presbyterian Church, Hardshaw-street. conducted a short service at Eccleston Grange, after which the cortege de- parted foi the cemetery. •The chief mourners were Alderman D. M'Eechnie..Niessrs. Daniel M'Kechnie, Alexander M'Kechnie, Duncan MK-chnie (sons), A.R. Norman, nuncorn, and David Goldsworth (sons-in-law). The Rev. J. Brown also condncted the service at the graveside. A large number of beautiful floral tributes were receivtd from sym- pathising friends.

THE session of Parliament which The Opening of Parliament. opened on Ttmsc'ay is to have short existence and an abrupt end` This, at all events, is what we are told by sorae writers and speakers whose dominating ambition seems to be the establishment of a reputation as political prophets. But as the predictions of thees same gentlemen have always been wrong so far, it is not prudent to pay very much attention t° their latest attempts to forecast the future. The very fact that the present Government still exist° to open another sass ion of Parlia-reent discredits all these dabblers in p olitical mete3rology. Ever/ one reraembere the confident assertions that tise

Liberal majority would fall to pieces within 0.11 months of the General Election. Yet how differ. ant has been its record. It has not only held together with splendid discipline in face of the attacks of its opponents, but it has also been able to accomplish some exceedingly useful legislatiOnt a very difficult task in face of the persistent or position of a large minority in the House °I Commons and of an overwhelming majority in the House of Lords. The same qualities which have : I kept the Government in office so far, will, it raaY be reasonably expected, carry them through the , present session, and at the end of it Place , to their credit another instalment of progres° sive legislation. The opening debates on TOW day were remarkable for the enunciation of seele singular political doctrines by the leaders of the Opposition. Lord SALISBURY now appears to have come to the conclusion that a Governtae°, which is supported by a comparatively fatal' majority should decline to hold office, and, Wai suppose, should dissolve Parliament. But Ler' SALISBURY should either not have gone so far ae, this, or he should have gone further. He shoula have explained what the next step would be, If/ after Parliament had been dissolved and a general ,', election had been held, there were still aalY a small majority for one or another of the partits. Does he hold that, under these circuinstances, constituencies should again be appealed to art " what he was pleased to consider a sufficieer . majority had been obtained ? Such a 11014_1e: - I that would be utterly impracticable, and in fact, soon bring the affairs of the country iate, -• estate of chaotic confusion. It was once declare' ~ by an eminent British statesman that, whatever else happened, the " Queen's Government" be carried on. Lord SALISBURY seems to be a a , different opinion, as he praetically maintains that : there should be no" Queen's Government" 1101e55 ' it is backed up by a majority of fifty or sixV, or; it may be a hundred, for he does ne . condescend to specify the precise numher,. i. with which he would be satisfied., This latea; : notion of " the Marquis" is,indeed,one of the ra°l3 peculiar which even he has ever ventured ea, ' formulate, and by gravely propounding it in b,15 ' opening speech in Parliament he very clear? showed how weak was the indictment he Woel).'ah ; to lay against the Government. It is an idea vilue .i this Government and probably no Governalent if : not even one headed by Lord SALISBURY hi a 1 : —will ever act upon. In the opinion of. raa74l , competent judges small Parliamentary raaJeritjv'e r, Will be more usual in the future than they baba been in the past. Governments will have te et , managed with sufficient ability and tact ta rgo.. •' along with them. In that respect, the Gave ..0 ment that is now in power have set a fine e%BP .. and have proved that it is not absolutely rierCrier ,! sary to have an overwhelming following 11l e ..0„ to accomplish legislation nf even a distinctly qr. gressive character. In the House of Comma" •eole Banroun made a declaration which was, n., enecie respects, even more singular than that of hie 11130 in the House of Lords. According to gr.
roun it is a" farce " to propose legislation whioh Will not pass the House of Lords, and he declares that the programme of proposed legislation which the Government submits to the House of Coin-
raons is not so arousing as a music hall adver-

tisement and not so instructive as the announce- sent of an academical course of discussion. In tine way Mr. BALFOUR degrades the House of Commons and elevates the House of Lords. In lus opinion a programme of legislation which is 4.lPported by a majority of the House of Commons a "mere farce" so long as it has net the approval of .the Peers. Sir WILLIAM HAncouar,in his reply aughtiwell ask the country to take mote of this declaration. It raises the issue, "Commons versus Lords,,, with unmislakeable clearness.

THE "Union of the Unionists "is „. Welsh olsestablishment apparently in a critical condition just now. We have previously cenunented upon the disagreements that have atissu between the two wings of the Unionist Party over the Irish Land Bill, and these dis- agreements have by no means been smoothes a!er yet. In fact, it is not at all improbable, 4,4°111d the Tories finally take up the cause of the landlords, that the differences will become so serious as to lead to a break-up of that "solid Xorth which has been one of the greatest abstacles iu the way of Home Rule. Another 2:"Sf3 of friction has suddenly been found in the Welsh Disestablishment Bill. If Tories have Prided themselves upon one thing above another It ia that they stand in politich for " Church and Stater with a preference for Church rather than state. Judge of their surprise, therefore, on "41ting up one morning this week to find that their tieliaPensable ally,Mr. CimmeserAiN,cooly rscom- "lands them to give up the Welsh Church disestablishment and to make the best terms ,"11.03, can with regard to the "loaves and fishes." a Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S opinion the Welsh Church la bound to be disestablished, and he seems to 411 ink that the clergy, in spite of all their loud 4. "elk about "sacrilege," and such like,may be easily Pacified with substantial slices out of the widow- Illents. This, surely, is an offence which will never , forgiven the leader of the Liberal Union- latB. After all the fine talk about high °tins and the maintenance of true i°", glen, are the defended of the Estab- )aarnents going to allow the whole subject to be de alt With as a matter of pounds, shillings and IZce• The bare suggestion is intolerable. Yet CH,MtnaeLAIN is clearly of opinion that it is tri a question of terms, and he has had a good ef communion with Tories lately.

Ir would seem that Wednesday 'rtiC Weather, was one of the coldest days on record. North and South in the 11;_t1tiall Isles the cold was intense, and in some "'dances the severity of the climatic conditions W4B added to by gales and snowstorms. As the ;hid blew from a south-easterly direetion the thald Coast has suffered most on this occasion, tregh not so heavily as the West Coast did in ge great storm of a few weeks ago. In the North hi Scotland, traffic on roads and railways was t:9°elted by snow, and at Dundee the gale regis- -4:"1 a velocity of seventy-eight miles an hour. " Southampton, the other extreme of the crtlntry, the docks were frozen over for the time in fourteen years, and near Ply- aill„(3tb a train was thrown off the metals by fteourriulation of snow. The destruction of the creatures of fell and moor is reported to be all large scale. Grouse have been starved to cath in large numbers on the Westmoreland hills aettd in the south of Scotland, and those that have ,tetir:lved have in many instances become almost 'eine as barn-door fowls, coming into the farm- -1041.43 and kitchen gardens to feed. It is feared, that in some of the more exposed pastoral f'ettutricts even the hardy mountain sheep will have treBll victims in considerable numbers to the ex- -14 `1,6 cold and drifting snow. In one district '8 ie North, children have even been snowed up tp4chec>l) and have had to be dug out and carried ; their homes in an exhausted condition. 4(1;8 needless to say that the weather has Tie Zed to the miseries of the unemployed who are, (1.113fi to all accounts, unusually numerous in of the country. 4tim. div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES. ICE ACCIDENT.-NARROW ESCAPE.

On Su-n-d—ai;lt-er-noon, about five o'clock, a boy, nine years of ago, named Walter Brown, son of Mr. Peter Brown, of the Rutter's Vaults, Brunswick-st., Runcorn, was sliding on the Big Pool, when be fell through a hole in the ice. Fortunately there were others skating on the ice at the time and they witnessed the accident. He was rescued from his perilous position by Mr. Shaw, of Mill Brow, and at once taken home.

div.head: ST. PAUL'S BIBLE CLASS, RUNCORN. – –
div.p: ST. PAUL'S BIBLE CLASS, RUNCORN. - -

The weekly meeting of this class on Sunday afternoon was well attended. Mr.B. Kniveton pre- sided, and gave a bible lesson, after which an in- teresting address was delivered by Mr. Wilding. An organ solo was given by Mr. Rowley, and Mr Gewanlock sang as a solo, "The song of Naaman: Mr. William Cooke presided at the organ.

div.head: TER WORE OF TYR DISTRICT NURSE.
div.p: TER WORE OF TYR DISTRICT NURSE.

From January 3rd to January 25th, there had been attended te by the district nurse 18 cases (six being fresh ones) as fellows :--Six chronic, two surgical, three typhoid, and seven medical. Of hese two were dead, cue had gene to a Liverpool Hospital, one to the School for the Blind, and one was well. This left 19 cases on the books. Nine- teen patients had received occasional visits. The number of visits paid to cases was 148; and the number of occasional visits, 42; total, 191. TETE AGED PEOPLE'S TREAT AT RUNCORN. . _

A.t..:1-ne-reirn-g of the Scrutiny and Provision Com- mittee for the Aged People's Treat, held on Friday evening, under the presidency of Mr. S. Taylor,d.P., it was decided to substitute for hot pot, which has ben formerly given at this treat, a meat tea. It was decided to give each man an ounce of tobacco, and each womas one ounce of tea, but the commit- tee will not provide mince pies as has been the custom on previous occasions. The following were appointed the purchasing committee :—Messrs. W. Shaw, T. Woods, T. Reynolds,Robinson, S.Coventry, aad Smith. _ _

div.head: ----• ANOTHIR MINCORN MAN MISSING. – –
div.p: ----• ANOTHIR MINCORN MAN MISSING. - -

It is supposed that John Roberts, of Queen-st., I Runcorn, aged 50 year., mate ef the steamer Swift, belonging to Messrs. Brundrit and Co., met his death by drowning, on Wednesday night week. The circumstances are as follows :—On the night in question he, accompanied by John Davies, went from the steamer to Beaumaris to poet letter. After spending a short time in the town Roberts returned to the boat. His companion not turning up, he started for the steamer himself. The water was very rough at the time, and it is thought that he fell overboard, for the boat was found next morning at Garth Ferry, about three miles away. The facts have been reported to the authorities. ANOTHER BURNING ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN. I A child, three years of age, named Harold Whit- field, who lived with his mother at 34. Loch-at., Runcorn, sustained serious injuries by burning on Friday morning, shortly before seven o'clock. The child's mother,whose husband was buried two days previously.was asleep in a bed in the kitchen when she was awakened by screams. She found the child's shlirt burning. She extinguished the fire immediately, and sent for a medical gentleman. Dr. McKenzie was soon in attendance, and found that the child had been seriously burnt about the abdomen and the right thigh. It is thought that the boy was warming himself at the ire when the accident occurred. HEARTLESS DESERTION OR CHILDREN IT RUNCORN.

At the Runcorn Police Court en Friday morning, before Mr. John Brundrit (chairman), and Mr. E. Imison, a middle-aged man named Edward Simp- son, who when arrested the previous day by F.C. Gregory was employed at some sewerage works at Cadishead, was charged with neglect of his family which had become chargeable to the common funds of the Runcorn Poor Law Guardians.—Mr. John Frodshain, who proved the csse on behalf of the Guardians, stated that about four years ago the prisoner deserted his family, and his two children were taken to the workhouse. One of them died on the 2nd January, this year, and the other was still chargeable to the Union. They had cost the Unioa about .£3O. The prisoner had ?sever made any enquiry concerning them, and they had been unable to ascertain his whereabouts until that week.—P.C. Gregory gave evidence as to appre- hending the prisoner at Cadishead the. previous day. The magistrates committed the prisoner to gaol for one month hard labour. BRUTAL ASSAULT ON A WIDNES CONSTABLE.

On Tuesday, at the Widnes Police Court, before Alderman Timmis and Councillor W. W. Gossage, a young man named James Doyle, of 72, Oxford- street, was charged with drunkenness and assault- ing Poliee-constable Hamilton. He was also charged with damaging the officer's uniform to the extent of Ils. 41, The prisoner himself had evidently suffered in the struggle, and he appeared in the dock with his head copiously bandavd. The con- stable found the prisoner drunk neara fire in Ox- ford-street, where some street improvements are in progress. He was lying with his legs under the tire, and was in considerable danger of being burnt. He refused to leave at the request of the watchman aud Hamilton ordered him away, but still he would net move. The officer seized hold of him, where- upon the prisoner struck him on the head and , knocked him to the ground, damaging his trousers in the fall. The prisoner then ran away, but was ' followed, and when overtaken by Hamilton, the prisoner's head was covered with blood, the wounds having been caused by falling about on the slippery ground.—The prisoner was mulcted in fines, costs, and damage amounting in all to £2 7s. 10d., with the alternative of twenty one days' imprisonment with hard labour. RUNCORN BOARD Or_ GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held in the Beard room at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. The chair was occupied by Mr. Mclntyre, J.P. In addition to the members of the Rural District Council being present there were the Revs. Canon Woods and Dr. Gaetaldi, Messrs. S. Taylor, J.P., Honeley, J.P., and J. Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (deputy clerk).—A lengthy circular letter on the subject of workhouse administration was submitted by the Clerk.—On the motion of Mr. Handley, it was unanimously decided that each member he provided with a printed copy of the communicalon.—Mr. Heywood proposed that the reports of tie relieving officers be considered im- mediately after the reading of the minutes instead of after the transaction of the business of the Board as at present.—Mr. Lewis seconded. and it was sup- ported by Mr. Baxter, Mr. Woodward, and Mr. Darbyshire.—Mr. Stokes and the, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi opposed the proposition.—On I,eing put to the vote the motion was lgst by 14 to 10 votes.—Mr. Stokes then proposed that a tire be provided in the ante- room for the benefit of the poor people who had to see the Guardians at the meeting.—Canort Wood seconded, and the motion was carried unanimously. —Mr. Heywood submitted the financial statrnent which showed that there was an increase in the amount given in relief. In Runcorn there had been distributed £O5; Frodshatn district £3B; Budworth district £2.s.—The report was adopted.—ThiS WaS all the business of public interest.

BAND OF HOPB DIRRTING AT RUNCORN. On Monday evening a Band :of :Hope meeting was held in the National Schools, Church-st., Run- corn, under the presidency of the Rev. H. B. Firth who gave the first part of an interesting story. Reci- tations and temperance selections were given by several members of the society. There was a good atteadance. div.head: EXAMINEE, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 9, 1895.
div.p: THE EXAMINEE, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 9, 1895.

RUNCORN CRICKET CLUB. This club held its annual meeting on Friday evening at Mr. Riley's assembly rooms, Bridge-st., Runcorn. Mr. M. Wright occupied the chair. TREASURER'S AND SECRETARY'S REPORTS. iMr. Edison, the treasurer, submitted the statement of accounts. The members' subscriptions had amounted to £9,the vice-presidents' donations £lO ss. fid. tennis club subscriptions £5 19s. 61., and gate receipts £8 12s. Bid., total £33 17s. sp. The expenses came to £2B 103. Id., leaving a balance in hand of £5 7s. 7id. The balance sheet was adopted, on the motion of Mr. Tickle,seconded by Mr. Nield.—Mr. G. S. Frith, secretary, submitted his report, in which it was stated that the past season had been disappointing as regarded result. Out of a total of 17, only two were won, 13 lost, and two drawn. The number of runs scored by their opponents was 1,303 for the loss of 151 wickets, average 8 63 runs per wicket ; the number obtained by Runcorn was 1,007 for the loss of 153 wickets, an average of 658 per wicket, which was two runs per wicket less than their opponents. The highest score made by any one player was 37 by Samuel Abrams against Northwich away. G. S. Frith beaded the first eleven batting averages, and William Gaskellthe secend eleven, for which the latter received a bat presented by Dr. McKenzie. • ELECTION OF OFFICERS. On the motion of Mr. Langshaw, seconded by Mr. Ellison, it was decided that Mr. Taylor be re-elected president, and references were made to the readiness with which that gentleman was willing te assist any- thing connected with sport. The vice-presidents were reappointed. The following officers were chosen : Captain let eleven, G. S. Frith; vice-captain, J. Tickle; hon. treasurer, Mr. H. Wright ; lion. secretary, Mr. S. Frith ; committee, Dr. McKenzie, Messrs. S. Abrams, W. Faulkner, VI,. Nie.d, W. S. Gaskell, J. E. Lang- ' shaw, J. Cragg, R. Jeaceck, H. Pope, J. Ellison and Thomas Moores.—The question as to whether arrange- ments should be made for holding sports for local athless was referred to the committee for their serious consideration.

PRESENTATION. The Chairman stated that at the commencement of the season Dr. McKenzie, with the okject of induciag the younger members of the A team to excel in cricket, promised to give a bat to the one who obtained the best average. This had been purchased, and on a silver plate was the inscription " Runcorn Cricket Club, 1894, presented by Dr. McKenzie to W. F. Gaskell, for best batting average."—Dr. McKenzie in making the presen- tation, said he would have great pleasure in subscribing for another bat next year, and to follow it up season by season. Perhaps some local gentleman would express his decision to present a ball to the best bowler.—Mr. Gaskell acknowledged the gift.

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

On Wednesday evening, a smoking concert was held in the Runcorn Liberal Club, when there was a good attendance. Mr. John Clarke occupied the chair. The programme included songs by Messrs. J. Parker Richard Green, John Hosker, A. Shingler, H. Wright, W. Wright, F. Massey, G. Rowley, T. Cooke, J. Joyce, and J. Stanway. A pianoforte duet was given by Messrs. G. and R. Bowser, and a duet Was contributed by Messrs. A. Riley and T. Cooke. BBTHESDA. CONGIEBOATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL,

div.head: It lINCOUN.
div.p: It lINCOUN.

In connection with this Sabbath school, a very successful social gathering of teachers and elder scholars was held on Thursday evening. About 50 persons were present. Business in connection with the school was transacted, and the appointment of officers was corlfirmed. The Pastor (Rev. J. Simp- son) presided. Mr. W. H. Chadwick was appointed superintendent ; Mr. Thomas Hanalley, treasurer; Mr. Harold Chadwick,secretary ; and Mr. C. Temple, missionary secretary. A vote of condolence was passed with Mr. C. C. Le Couteur in his recent sad I bereavement. SHAILENS' INSTITUTE, RTJFICORIC The Holy Trinity Church choir, Runcorn, pro- vided the programme at the weekly entertainment at the Seamen's Institute, Runcorn, on Tuesday evening. There was a large attendance. A mis- cellaneous programme arranged by Mr. Lancaster' was submitted and admirably gone through. Songs were given by Miss Bradshaw, Master F. Timmins, Messrs. Shingler, Findlow, Morris, Turner and Atherton. Two pianoforte solos were well ex- ecuted by Nire.Bartram, and the recitations by Miss Emma Turner and Mr. /1 ulse greatly pleased the audience. Mr. Clare rendered a cornet solo. Three sailors also contributed itema.to the programme. I

div.head: RYNCORM GAS COMPANY.
div.p: RYNCORM GAS COMPANY.

The half-yearly meeting of this Company was held at the registered offices of the Cempany on Thursday morning. Mr. F. Rigby (Chester) occu- pied the chair. The directors' report to the share- holders stated that the depressed condition of the trade of the town had interfered with the consump- tion of gas. The revenue account showed a profit of £4,303 2s. 31. for the year,as against £386 188.1 d. for the year 1893. In order to pay the interest on debentures and declare a dividend of ten per cent.a further sum of £202 Is. 103. would be required. This it was proposed to charge against the balance standing to profit and loss account, leaving a credit balance of £528 3s. sd. to that account. The report was adopted. It was decided to contribute twenty tons of coke to the Distress Fund during February, and if necessary, the same quantity during March.

BRTHESDI CONORRGA-TIONAL- CHURCH. The members of the children's class in connection with Bethesda Congregational Church gave a mis- cellaneous concert in the schoolroom on Wednesda3 evening, the chair being taken by Mr. J. Speakman After a few opening remarks by that gentleman, the children proceeded to entertain their audience with a very varied and lengthy programme consist- ing of dialogues, solos, action songs, recitations and pianoforte solos. These were rendered in a raanner calculated to reflect much credit on those concerned in their training. At the close of the meeting a vote of thanks was passed to the chairman for the ntost genial and interesting manner in which he had fulfilled his office; also to the Rev. J. Simpson and his helpers for the programme most ably prepared for the entertainment of the audience, and in the rendering ef which it was most evident that the youthful performers were highly pleased with their little endeavours.

THE DISTRESS .A.T RUNCORN. The bitterly sold weather which has prevailed during the week has increased the distress in the town, and the application to the ward committees for relief are more numerous. The meeting of the general committee was held on Thursday evening, when the following subscriptions were reported ; Rev. Canon Wood, £5; Manchester ship Canal,.£2s ; proceeds of the concert by the Negro Nomads, Liverpool, .216 15s. 101. ; Mr. Walter Cellier,.£3 3s. ; Mr. J. Evershed, M P., per Mr. W. R. Wass, ..£2 25.; Dr. Steele, £2 25.: Mr. John Simpson, £2; Mr. Jol- liffe, .£1 Is.; Mr. Thomas Moores. £l. Free break- fasts have again been given ;at the Greenway-road Board schools and the National schools. A soup kitchen for the benefit of seamen and their children was opened at the Seamen's Institute, Runcorn, on Thursday. A number of esildren were on Monday evening, provided with a substan- tial tea in the Trinity schools.—On the Irwell-lane enclosure, on Thursday afternoon, an association football match was played, the proceeds of which were in aid of the Runcorn Unemployed Fund. The match was between the Runcorn Association Club and the Liverpool Licensed Victuallers. After a well contested game the match ended in a draw, neither side scoring. A HUSBAND DESERVEDLY PUNISHED. At the Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, before Messrs. T. Handley and E. lmison, George Fryer, late of Weston Point, was brought up under a war- rant issued on the complaint of his wife, Mary, for arrears on an order made under the Married Women's Act of the 12th of February, 1894, for her maintenance. - Mrs. Fryer stated that on the occa- sion the order was made, she was living with her husband, when he assaulted her, for which offence he was fined. An order was also made for their separation, she being given the custody of the four children. Since then she bad removed to Runcorn, but her husband had never made the least inquiry concerning her, whilst she and her children were almost starving. He was owing 51 week& pay- ments,which amounted to .£3B ss. P.C. Richardson said that he apprehended him at Birkenhead. Prisoner admitted owing the amount, but stated that he was unable to pay. The magistrates con- sidered the case a bad one,and sent prisoner te gaol for three months, whereupon prisoner exclaimed, "This is justice in England." PIIIILITIVE METHODIST CHIPXL, RENCORN. The Rev. W. Albert, of Winsford, occupied the pulpit at this place of worship on Sunday, when sermons were preached on behalf of the Home, Colonial, and Foreign Missions. There were good congregations, and the collections realised a satis- factory amount. The choir rendered a special anthem at the evening servise.—On Wednesday evening there was a large attendance in the schoolroom' when the annual missionary meeting was held. The chair was occupied by Mr. C. Hill, and there were also on the platform Revs. T. Bramall, H. Didcock, and D. Albert.—Fhe Rev. H. Didcock submitted a financial statement for the past year.! the Primitive Methodist Home,Colonial, and Foreign Missionary Society. Ile said,like other societies, they bad, last year, a diminished income. but that was accounted for by the commercial de- pression, and the coal strike. They, however, finished the year with a balance in hand of £238 Bs. 11d.—The Rev. T. Bramall and the Rev. David Albert also addressed' the meeting.--it was stated that over .£6 had been collected towards the funds of the society from that church. Votes of thanks having been passed the meeting concluded. div.head: OUDFHLLOWS.
div.p: OUDFHLLOWS.

The annual meeting of the committee of manage- ment of the Grand United Order of Oddfellowe was held at the Rising Sun Lodge, Halton Castle, on Monday. There were present : Bros. Job Hancock, W. Lea, T. Booth, R. Hughes, and 0. Hazleburet (trustees), T. Davies (tress.), W. Massey (sec.), and Brothers W. Moston, W. B. denes, 0. Rutter, .1. Douglas, F.J. Massey, J. W. Bosworth, W. Moores, and W. Lambert. The secretary read his annual report which stated that during the year,ten mem- bers had died, 26 had been struck off for various causes, and 56 had entered, which gave a net gain of 20 members. The membership now good at 942. .E. 213 12s. 2d. bad been received in contributions, and £36 Is. sd. interest, and £94 ha a been paid for the deazh of ten members, .£6O for the death of members' wives; £8 for the death of a widow. The funeral fund now stood at £990 2*. lid. The management expenses were £l9 17s. 3id., which left a balance ip hand of Bs. 91 The increase in funds during the year on the funeral fund was £93 15s. Oid. The total worth of the three lodges comprising the district was £5,621 I3s. sid. It was stated that the total increase in the funds of the district lodges during the year was £370 17. The accounts having been passed, the elect ion of officers was proceeded with and was as tollows: D.M.. Bro. Lea; D. D.M., Bro. Lambert ; auditor, Bro. Moors; the trustees, treasurer ano secretary were re-,dected. Bros. James Banner, G. Rutter, W. Moores, Job Hancock, W. Di oston, W. B. Jones, with the district officers were appointed as the Juvenile Committee ot Management.—Bro. Hughes proposed, and Bro. Hancock seconded, that Bro. Massey be nominated for the post of G.S. of the order. but hs declined to stand.—Votes of thanks zoncluded the meeting.

div.head: GRAYING DO-OK QUESTION AT
div.p: THE GRAYING DO-OK QUESTION AT
RUNCORN.

THE TRADHS' SOCIETIES DEPUTA lONS. The Parliamentary and General Purposes Committee of the Runcorn Urban District Council received deputa- tions on Tuesday evening from several departments of trade in Runcorn, to hear their views with regard to the counter proposals of the late Board of Commissioners regarding the graving dock question. The chair was occupied by Mr. Philip Speakman, J.P., C.C., and there were present : Rev. Dr. Gastaldi,Dr. McKenzie.Meszre. J. W. Lightburn, J. Pritchard, D. Bisbrown, J. Wilson, W. M. Williams, E. Imison, J.P. W. Collier, T. Dean, G. Hewitt, H. J. Grice, J. Fl. Kirkham, S. Taylor, J.P., F. Wiswall and M. Sweetman. The representatives of the dock labourers, Messrs. Abrams Lambert, and Gandy, were first admitted and explained the views of the dock labourers on the question. They were strongly in favour of increased lay-by facilities for shipping. Their object was to get ships in the first place to Runcorn,and after- wards to consider the question of the graving dock. They considered that a lay-by would be preferable to a graving dock, but at the same time they would be pleased to see both schemes carried into effect.—Mr. H. Branch representing ths boilermakers expressed their opinions on the subject which were favourable to the carrying out of the agree- ment existing between the authority and the Ship Canal Company, which was solely for the provision of a grav- ing dock. The shipwrights representatives. Messrs. Well, Findlow, Taylor and Key argued that it was an imperative necessity that the graving deck, as set forth in the agreement, should be constructed. If, however, it could be placed on the western side of Runcorn Bridge instead of the situation mentioned in the agreement, it would be better for all concerned.—Mr. Millington, on behalf of the ship brokers, expressed the opinion that it would be to the advantage of Runcorn, if increased facilities could be provided for the convenience et vessels coming to the port. They could at a later stage go in for the construction of the graving dock as men- tioned in the agreement.—Mr. Gatley. secretary Of the Watermen's and Porters' Association said that those on whose behalf he appeared were not in anyway selfish, but at the same time they were anxious that the pelicy of the ehipwrights should receive the earnest considera- tion of the cocrimittee.—Mr. Stubbs, a master ship- wright said he was in favour of increased facilities mentioned in the proposals, and the postponement of the carrying out of the agreement, as desired by the old Board of Commissioners.—After the various deputation, had been heard, the committee considered the subjects and they ultimately decided that Mr. Lake, the law I clerk, should forward to the directors of the Manchester Ship Canal Company the counter-proposals suggested by the Council's predecessors to those set forth by Mr. Collier. These have already been published. The ques- tion of dues was introduced during the interviews, and it was contended that Runcorn should have the same privileges as enjoyed by Ellesmere Port and Weston Point. The committee, however, seeing that the Canal Company had already issued a circular to the elect that pottery material up to 400 tons would be allowed to go up the canal free of dues, they determined not to intro- duce the matter into the proposal.

div.head: RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

HALY YEARLY MEETING. On Tuesday evening, in Lacey-street schoolroom, Widnes, the half-yearly meeting of the Runcorn Co- operative Society was held. Mr. D. Worthington occu- pied the chair, and he was supported by Messrs. Bolt, W. Cropper, J. fietney, J. Sayle, E. Aston, J. Rogerson, J. Evans (general manager and cashier), and William Upton (secretary). The report of the committee which was published in the last issue of the " Examiner " was submitted. At the outset the Chairman referred to a letter which had appeared in a local paper, signed "F. H.," which he stated was misleading. Be thought that anyone connected with the society ought to come to their meetings and make inquiries SO that he might get facts correctly, before rushing into print. The writer in the communication endeavoured to show that more business was transacted at the shops in Widnes than in Runcorn. But he (the chairman) wished to state that the figures for Runcorn did not include the out branches of Weston and Frodshara, whereas those tor Widnes included both Appleton and Simms Cross. If they took Runcorn RS a whotelhey found that in the grocery department the amount taken was £18,126 ss. 11d.; whereas in Widnes, including Siinms Cross it was £15,914,185. 21. leaving a balance in favour of Run- corn of £2,211 78.90. The total purchases at Runcorn, Weston, and Frodstiam stood at £23,961 191. 9d., and Widnes. Simms Cross and Appleton £20,710 153. 50. or £3,251 ts. 30. in favour of the former town. (Ap- plause.) He deprecated the antagonism that appeared to exist against the Runcorn portion of the society. Although they had their establishments on the Lanca- shire aide, yet it was the Runcorn society which estab- lished them. He stated that Runcorn did not take a single shilling from Widnes, it was all returned to them in the shape of dividend. In conclusion he spoke of the increase in the sales and to the general advancement the society was making. The balance sheet was under con- sideration for more than two hours, many questions being asked to which answers were given by the Chair- man, secretary, and the auditor. In the course of the discussion Mr. Poulson expressed a hope that the wages account would not in any way be reduced although they might curtail their expenditure in other depart- ments. He referred to the poor salaries paid to their principal officers and eventually gave notise of motion that at the next half-yearly meeting, he would move that their salaries be increased. It was decided that the Ship Canal shares held by the society shonld be included in the financial statement at current prices. k long argument took place with regard to the interest made in connection with the investments in the wholesale society, Mr. Poulson contending that the interest should have been included in the amount disposable for dividend so that the present members in a period of distress such as existed at the present time might have the advantage, instead of its being capitalised for the benefit of future generations. It was decided that no delegates be sent to any conferences connected witn the co-operative movement with the exception of those associated with the business of the society. The Chairman announced that a requisition had been received from a number of persons at Widnes, asking for a special meeting to be convened in that town to consider the alteration of rules. On examination, it was found that the signa- tories were not members of the Society ; therefore it had not received the required attention. Another requisition had been handed in, which was a very lengthy docu- ment, and in the effect that rule three should he altered, that the half-yearly meetings should be held alternately at Runcorn avid Widnes, and that the committee should c insist of eight member.. four elected !row: earth plas ‘. div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN. (BY AN OCCASIONAL CONTRIBUTOR).
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN. (BY AN OCCASIONAL CONTRIBUTOR).

lam pleased to find that the recently formed Earlestown and District Liberal Association are bestirring themselves in a practical manner, and are taking steps to make the public acquainted with the fact that there is an organisation in ex- istence prepared to look after their interests. They have issued a circular addressed to the Liberals of Earlestown in which they state that the unsatis- factory state of the Liberal organisation in the dis- trict has led the-u to take up the wot kin the hope that they may receive the active and cordial sup- ' port of all who are interested in the programme of reform to which the Liberal party has pledged itself. Three objects are stated, but the most im- portant of the three to my mind is " To promote the return of Liberal representatives to Parliament and local governing bodies." Tois is as it ought to be, and it is only a pity that the association did not take such active measures earlier; had they done so, the election to the District Council might have assumed a different complexion. Much good! work has certainly been neglected, but it is nevgi, too late to mend, and I hope the fruits of the work of the association will be shown at tee next election to the District Council.

Another important and sensible feature in con- nection with the Association is its democratic principle and the endeavour to place its advantages within the reach of even the poorest working-man. The subscription has been fixed at the low sum of one shilling per annum. This, the Committee feel will make it possible for almost every man to take his part in the work that is about to be inaugu- rated. They further state that the present situation of the Party in the district makes it imperative that there should be n 3 further delay, but that the objects of the Association be at once vigorously pursued, until the organization is in a satisfactory condition, and able to render effective service whenever the occasion should arise. Such a work as this should not be taken up in a half-hearted way, but should be pushed forward with a thoroughness that will enable the Committee to accomplish the task they have set themselves.

The severe weather which 'has prevailed for the past week has unfortunately not departed without claiming one victim in this district. A good sheet of ice is no doubt very tempting to healthy lads, but when that ice is ant considered safe, it is foolishness to ri,k life upon it. Yet on Sunday. although notices were put up warning people that the ice on Newton lake was dangerous, it was with the utmost difficulty that the lake-keeper could prevent a number of lads from going on it. Only one result could be expected if they persisted in venturing upon the ice, and on Monday morning the worst fears were unfortunately realised. The ice when it broke was found in that particular spot to be only a quarter of au inch thick,aud those lads who heeded the warning of the lake-keeper may be thankful that they diel so, or they might have shared the same fate as the poor lad who lost his life on Monday.

The proceedings at the District Council on Mon- day were conducted a little more decorously than at the former meeting, but whether this was due to the presence of some of the public or not, I cannot, of course. say. There were one or two slight breezes, but nothing of any moment. A long dis- cussion took place over the issue of a notice calling attention to the existing bye-lavv with regard to obstructions on the footpath, and to the cleansing away of snow. This discussion really should not have taken place, as the surveyor was only acting in accordance with the instructions laid down. I see also that the qaestion of lighting was brought up by the Committee, and arrangements made for the representatives of each ward to inquire and report what further lamps are required in their respective wards. This is an important subject, for, there is not the slightest doubt that in several parts of the district the lighting is sadly deficient, whilst in some of the wards there is not a single lamp in sores portions of then), and in neighbourhoods where a gas lamp would be an unmixed blessing.

There is a question I have not heard rnentiened lately, and that is the proposed post office. I hope it has net been shelved, but that it vt ill shortly be brought up, and pushed forward with the ut- most vigour. We want both a postal and telegraph office, and these we must have sooner or later, no matter wko pays for them.

div.head: CHILDREN'S ENTERTAINMENT AT NEWTON.
div.p: CHILDREN'S ENTERTAINMENT AT NEWTON.

On Saturday evening the children of St. Peter's School gave their fifth annual entertainment in the Town Hall at Newton. As on previous occasions tlsts hall was crowded to excess, and doubtless the financial results will be squally as satisfactory. The first part of the programme was devoted with one exception to the in- fant portion, the opening speech being cleverly given by Jessie Lewis. The next was an action song entitled " The busy mother," given by a number of girls, in which they depicted the trials of a very husv woman. A musical drill with bannerettas was executed with imsa.z- ing precision and neatness, considering how very young the children were. An action song, "The Sailors:" by a number of infant hays was well given,and a dialogue by I Rig little girls, " The six little nurses" each of whom nursed a doll, created much amusement, their girls per- forming their tasks in a remarkably clever manner, the result being that gin was not so good for children, as cinder tea. Kindergarten games by the Infants were cleverly carried out, and showed the excellent training to which the 'youngsters had been aubmiVed. Mrs. Jarlev's waxworks, illustrating such characters as Miss loduffitt. Mother Huhbarci,Little Jack Horsier, Cinderella, Bo Peep, Jack Sprat. Simple Simon kc., WAN a source of much merriment. Miss Cassie Hayes officiated as Mrs. Jarley and explained the various qualities of her figures, whilst, Milly Wilkinson acted as the servant Angelina. The closing speech was very well delivered by" Miss Jarley," various local allusions being interpolated. The children were under the care of Miss Liptrott, who deserves every praise for the efficiency of her training. The second part of the programme consisted of a chil- dren' a operetta entitled " Idle Ben." The characters wthre " Idle Ben" (Willie Haynes), "The Beadle of Bees_ wick " (Frank Squire), " Awful Example" (Walter Strange), " Fairy Queen" (Annie Ellairi), Goblins : Tom Gee (Grimble), Tom Cooke,/Fred Denning, Prank Fletcher, Frank Harrison, Albert Lyons, Charles Mayor, Harold Mayor. There were also a large number of Jolly Boys and Girls, Cobblers and Farmers, besides a strong chorus of singers. The dresses were very neat and appropriate, those of the Goblins being especially so. The scene openeil at the Village Green at Beeswick where the Beadle enters, and announces that it is their intention to endeavour to amuse the audience, the choir singing "If you'd be healthy." Six school children followed on and after recounting the fun they indulged in, Rix cobblers enter and at ince proceed to business, singing the while. These give place to the farmers' boys who tell what their occupation is, an as a wind up a masherooraes in,who in answerto questions, says he is an awful example of what boys may become, but he is really the attendant on the " Fairy 'Queen." Idle Bert afterwards put in an appearance, his attire and general get up clearly indicating that he is an idle, worthless lad, and the chorus tell hint as much, in song. Ben is disgusted at his wretched condition,and says that none of the boys or girls will play with him. The Queen hereupon enters, and is welcomed by the assembled villagers, and asks what she can do for her subjects, and the Beadle introduces Ben, and sake her to use her influence with him. This she consents to do and asks the Beadle not to interfere with him. The next scene is supposed to be among the mountains, where Ben is di... covered who although he has forgotten his breakfast, is in high glee that he has no work to do. He soon begins to feel hungry and in the midst of his cosnplainings the Goblins enter, who twine a mystic spell around him, end he goes to sleep. Here he is discovered by some school , children who summon the Beadle. Ben is ultimatgly roused and bemoans his hungry and wretched condition.' The Queen is asked to intercede and she removes tile spell, and Ben gives an assurance that in future he will do his fair share of work, and will not be idle again. The concluding chorus of " Hurrah for Idle Ben," was effectively given,and in fact were all the other choruses. Evil' character performed his or her part with ability, and frequently gained the hearty applause of the audi- ence. The task of training the children must have been a gigantic one, and Mr. Singleton and his assistants are to be congratulated on the success of their efforts. The entertainment was repeated on Monday night when the Hall was again filled.

There was a large attendance, and at the close upwards of 80 persons enrolled themselves as members. Mr. Thotnas Wallington (secretary, Wycliffe P.S.A. Warringtun) was also present and gave useful assist- ance.
ItUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

On Thursday morning, the monthly meeting of this Council was held in the Town Hall, Runcorn. Mr. E. Imison, J.P., occupied the chair, and there were also present: Rev. Dr. Qastaldi, Dr. McKenzie, Messrs. P. Speakman, J.P., C.C.' S. Taylor, J.P., F. Wiswall, H. Grice, J. Pritchard, W. 'Collier, J. Wilson, G. H. Kirkham, G. Hewitt, W. M. Williams, D. Bisbrown, S weetman, J. W. Lightburn, T. Dean, and R. H. Pos- nett : Mr. F. A. Lake (law clerk), Mr. E. Marshall (secretary), Dr. McDougall (medical officer), and Mr. M. Barker (surveyor). MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. The report submitted by Dr. McDougall stated that the number of deaths registered during the past month amounted to twenty-two. Three were inquest cases, and of the remaining nineteen, two were due to scarla- tina, four to bronchitis, two to cancer, and one each to child birth, heart disease, diphtheria, membraneous croup, meningitis, diarrhoea, pneumonia, aneurism, apoplexy, paralysis, and one of dentition. Twenty-two deaths showed an average death rate for the 12 months of 13 08, and exclusive.of the inquest cases of 12 per thousand of the estimated population. The death rate for the past month was calculated on a reduced estimate of population, and if the census of 1891 were taken as a basis of calculation, the death rate would be at the rate of 10.04 for the twelve months.—The report was adopted. BIdIETTAYB AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEE. This committee recommeladed that a reply be sent to the Runcorn Postmaster's letter asking it it would be any public disadvantage if the sub-post office at No. 6, High-at., was closed on Wednesdays at 1 p.m., stating that the Council is of opinion that it would not, be to the disadvantage of the public if such office was closed at the time named.—Mr. T. C. Williams, having made application that the Council will allow him to pave the passage bellied his premises in Ivy-at. with bricks, and will adopt part of Ivy-st. if he makes it as far as his property extends, it is recommended that the Council sanction the paving of the said passage with bricks subject to those in the centre being put on edge and the work being done to the satisfaction of the surveyor,but with regard to the making of Ivy-st.,it is recommended that he be informed that the Council will not adopt part of a street but if the owners arc prepared to have the street made co-extensive with the laud built upon, the Council will be prepared to entertain a proposal from them.—That the work sif carrying out the Lowland- road improvement be proceeded with.—That the lamp opposite the Elms, High-road, be put in a more con- venient position. The Highways and Buildings Committee recommended that the plan of Mr. H. Dodd for the conversion of a house at the corner of Egerton-street and Handley-street, into a shop be approved.—That the plan of Dr. Robin- son of additions to a house in the Belvedere be aoproved.--The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Taylor, seconded by Mr. Bisbrown.

div.head: HEALTH COMMITTEE.
div.p: HEALTH COMMITTEE.

It was recommended by this committee that the appli- cation of Thomas Coffee to be registered as a keeper of a cemmon lodging-house at Nos. 1 and 2 Back Mersey-st. be rejected, on the ground that there are no back yards to such premises and that the water closet is situated 18 yards from the howes.—That the plan of the Trustees of the Ellesaaere-street Chapel for the abatement of a nuisance at the school connected with such chapel be approved.—That the plan of Mr. Thomas Plant of alter- ations to shop premises in High-st be approved.—The minutes were adopted.

div.head: PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: THE PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.

Tbe Health Committee recommended that Mr. Wis- wall, Mr. Lightburn, and the Law Clerk be the repre- sentatives of this Council at a sneeti»g in Manchester of various authorities interested as riparian authorities in the constitution of a Port Sanitary Authority for the Manchester Ship Canal.—Carried.

div.head: WATER COMMITTAL
div.p: WATER COMMITTAL

This committee recommended that arrangements he made with the river Weaver trustees for them to supply ships with water at Weston Paint through a stand pipe meter, such meter to be inspected quarterly by one of the CounciP3 servants and the quantity registered to be charged to the trustees.—The minutes were adopted.

div.head: VIE EXECUTION OY TNE CANAL BOATS ACT-.
div.p: VIE EXECUTION OY TNE CANAL BOATS ACT-.

The Markets Committee reported that the Secretary had prepared the following report as to the execution of the Canal Boats Act:—" I beg to present to you a report as to the execution of the Canal Boats Acts, 1877, 1884, and the obeervation of the regulations thereunder, tor the year ended 31st December, 1894. Fourteen beats have been registered during the year, nine of which were new boats, and 11 regiatered because of structural alterations, making a total of 977 registered in Runcorn. There have been 20 contraventions of the Acts and of the regulations thereunder reported by the Inspector. The particulars of the infringements are as follows :-11 boats without certificates on board; 4 boats with certi- ficates which did not identify owners • 2 boats out of repair and required to be painted; 2 boats overcrowded; 1 boat with number defaced. There have been no legal proceedings taken in respect of these infringements. The Inspector has reported to the authority that the defects complained of have all been remedied. 308 inspections have been made during the rear. There were found on board the boats 480 men, 130 women, and 151 children. Boys, 74 ; girls, 47 ; and 31 babies. Alterations have been made in certificates as follows :-5 certificates with names of owners altered ; 1 certificate with name of boat altered. There were two cases of sickness noti- fied under the Infectious Diseases (Notification) Act. 1889, as haying occurred on canal boats named " Gog and" Magog." Immediately on receipt of the notifica- tion, our Sanitary Inspector 'endeavoured to find the boats with a view to having them disinfected, but found that they had left for Wigan. That Authority were advised that the boats required disinfection. In the report for 1893 the number of women found on board Ithe boats inspected had increased, but this year it is satisfactory to note that they have decreased, there be- ing 6 women fewer and 4 children. There were 27 more men than in 1893. The salary of the Inspector is £2O per annum, with an allowance of 2s. per boat examined for registration. I have the honour, :to be, my Lords and Gentlemen, your obedient servant, E. MAusuratt, Secretary. The Local Government Board, White- hall, S.W."—Dr. Gastaldi drew attention to the fact that there were 182 children living on boats. The majority of these were deprived of proper education, and this should not be permitted.—The matter was, however, pot carried any further, and the minutes were adopted.

The questiou of tiling the vacancy was left to the comatittee.—The Technical Instruction Sub-Committee recommended that a deputation be appointed to visit technical insti- tutes in other towns, the cost of such not to exceed six or seven guineas.—Dr. Gastaldi moved an amendment that the expenses to be allowed should be £3.—Mr. Bisbrown seconded. div.head: BEFORE THL MAGISTRATES:
div.p: BEFORE THL MAGISTRATES:

A LOCAL BAKER SUMMONED FOR CRUELTY TO A HORSa. Yesterday morning at the Borough Police Conti., Mr. Johnson. 33, Rolleston-street, was charged wide having on the 14th January unlawfully and cruelly illtreatinga horse by working the same while in an unfit state, tand John Eckersley, 85, Bridge-street was charged with causing the same to be worked.—Johnson pleaded guilty, and Eckersley not guilty.—Sergeant Rowbot am stated that on Monday, the 14th January, he wastin Bridge-street when he saw the defendant driving a covered van with a bay horse which was lame on the off fore foot. He followed until the van stopped at Mr. Eckersley's shop. Johnson then told witness that he was the driver and was aware that the horse was lame. Its foot was very tender and on P.C. Lewis coming up Mr. Eckersley asked them to come and look at the horse, which was his. On Tuesday the 16th,in company with Inspector Luff,witnesss saw the horse again. Mr.Ecker- sley then told them he did not know the horse was outon the day in question as it was for sale.—P.C. Lewis con- firmed last witness's statement and Inspector Luff, R.S.P.C.A. deposed that when he saw the horse it was very lame in the off fore foot which washot and painful. Mr. Eckersley had cautioned Johnson a few days before the offence about working the horse. IR Court Mr. Eckersley said the horse was suffering free, a corn and was then on sate. On Tuesday he saw J orison driving it over Bank Quay bridge and noticed it was lame, tell- ing Johnson to get the horse's corn cut.—A tine of the costs was imposed in each case. A YOUTHFUL DEFENDER.—THE DESTRUCTION OF PROPERTY. Yesterday at the Borough Police Court before Mr. J. H. Fleming (chairman) and Councillor H. Roberts, John Healey ,'l2), Pierpoint-street was charged with assault- ing John Leigh, Lilford-street, en the 21st January.— Mr. A. Browne,soliciter. appeared to prosecute on behalf of the Property Owners'Association because considerable damage had been done to property around 11:wseybridge He said that on the day of the assault someone threw some stones at complainant's door and he went out and followed defendant home and complained totals mother. The boy then struck him on the head with a bottle, breaking the latter and causing the Com- plainant to go to the infirmary. Mr. Browne understood that during the last 12 months over 209 panes of glass had been broken in that neighbourhood. It was in consequence of this that he prosecuted in this case, and he wanted the defendant to be made an example of. The defendant and his mother both stated that when complainant came to the house he knocked her down and the by added that he had struck the man because his father was not there to take her part.—The bench dismissed him with a caution. NEGLECT OF FAMILY. At the Borough Police Court, yesterday, before Mr. J. H. Fleming and Councillor Roberts, Matthew and Elizabeth Carley, 66, Dallam-lane, were charged with having on the 24th January and on other dates in the last three months unlawfullyneglected fivechildreniunder the age of 16.—Mr.J.D. Buckton prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C., and stated that defendant worked at Dallam forge, and was the father of 11 children, five of whom were under 16. These live were the ones the de- fendants were charged wi! h neglecting, the case having been under observation for two or three months. Inspector M'Ateer,N.S.P.C.C., deposed that on the 24th of January he, in company with P.C. Williamson,visited the defendants' house, and found the five children in a deplorable condition. He examined each of the children personally, and Sarah (9), wore one dirty frock and a portion of a very filthy chemise, and no bosts or stock- ings. Catherine (8) was in the same unclothed state, and did not appear to have been washed for a long time. The boy Henry, and Agnes, were concealed upstairs, and when brought down, witness saw that the by wore a pair of raggY trousers and a vety dirty shirt. He was also very emaciated. The girl, (5) was also poorly clothed, and her body was covered with vermin bites, and the same applied to the boy Abel. Fie asked the woman to account for it and she said, " I am in delicate heal'h and have a sore leg." Witness examined the kitchen and found eine table and a broken chair or two, and the room did not appear to have been cleaned at all. Up- stairs there were two other rooms, one occupied by de. fendanes married daughter and one child, and the other had one bed, two old ticks, and sow e filthy sheets. In tins romp, the two defendants, Ihe live children, and a hoy of 16 slept. Witness visited the house again on the 29rh, accompanied by P.C. Meacock, and found every- thins in the same condition. He had spoken to the woman about her condition many times during the last three months, but it was no use. The male defendant' earned 30e. a week, arid the bow of 16. us., and from inquiries he had found that the husband was a 11 working man who gave hia money to his wife. The wife spent it in the public-house and he had been told that she sent for drink six or seven times a day.—P.C. Meacoek corroborated the inspector's statement alrnit the condition of the. house and children. During the detailing of His evidence Ihe female defendant behised in a very disorderly fashion, frequently interrupting with such remarks as " Your'e a liar," etc. It was flQt, until she was threetened with an incarceration of 24 hours in gaol before the hearing of the case that she cooled dowc.—The l'ench decided to aiiiourn the case

_ for a month. AN AETTUt FEIIALE PICKPOCKET. At the Borough l'olicec!..urt, on Wednesday morning, before Mr. .Tohta Fairclongh and other magistrates. In conversation with complainant prisoner asked him to buy her a shawl, and at a shop near the Centri.l Station he paid 10a. 1.1. d, for one and gave it to her. They then went to the station with the ' intention of going to Manchester but no train being then available they went to a public house and had some more beer. *Potting his hand int., his trousers pocket to pay for this the complainant found his purse was gone and accused the woman tatting it. Prisoner then ran away and complainant vas unable to catch her. He gave information to the polio., and Sergeant Cheney from complainant's description apprehended prisoner. and took her to the police statjon. She was then seached and one a littlo money found upon her, but concealed in her dress was a fournenny pieco which complainant ntiii lis tie he hail ITld a few years.— Complainant him.elf was I piralled and to his sur- prise the purse was found in his jtcket pocket •mptv, which provetthat the prisoner was an expert pick- pocket—The complainan,, Te.mas Mac. corroborated Mr. Hunt and demanded the back.—The Bench, however, said they had no sympathy with him, and ordered that Ca the sh owl lied tisen gi'en to her she should retain it and ,go to irl for 14 days' hard labour for the theft. resided at 148, Knutsford-road. On the day in question the boy went to school, and after the school hours were over missed his coat, and another coat belonging to a fellow-scholar was also missing. Nothing was heard of the coats until Friday last when the complainant noticed a boy named William Boswell at school wcaring his coat. He told the schoolinaster,who took possession of the coat and sent for Detective Monaghan, who made inquiries and found that the mother of Boswell had bought the coat from Mrs. Leslie's pawnshop, in Mersepst., and from there it was traced to Duckworth, toe defendant. The latter told Monaghan that be had found the coats in the sehool yard. Mr.Dobson said his client had been employed at St. James' for over 20 years as cleaner of the premises. He was a person who might be described as half-witted, the loss of his wife some years ago had a great effect upon him. His age was 66 or 89,and he had never been convicted of anything of this nature before. Ultimately a conviction was recorded against Duck- worth, who was then allowed toga.

STEALING A HEART. At the Borough Police Court on Thursday morning, before the Mayor (Councillor James Fairclough) and Alderman T. Sutton, Frederick M,inton, pork butcher, Nottingham, and Henry Foster, pork butcher, Birming- ham, were charged with stealing from the shop of Frederick John Carlisle, butcher, Market Place, about 4.30 on Wednesday afternoon, a cow's heart, value le 84.—Mr. S. Hunt (chief constable) stated that on Wednesday afternoon, Detective-Sergeant Monaghan and P.C. Barlow noticed the two defendants moving about the market very suspiciously. At length both went to Mr. Carlisle's shop and Manton going in asked the boy In charge the price of a cow's heart which was on the counter, and on being informed that it was is. Bd. Manton said that they knew the "boss" very well and would take the heart which could be booked to Charley Brown. Manton handed the heart to Foster who was outside the shop and told him to go off with it. This however the boy objected to and running out took the heart from under Foster's arm. Beth defendants then went to Mr. Bower's shop, but the officers thinking that they had seen enough arrested defendants and bronght them down. When charged at the police station Man- ton said "I've stolen nowt," and Foster made no reply. —The magistrates sent Manton to gaol for one month's hard labour and Foster for 14 days, corroborative evidence having been given by Frederick John Carlisle, jun., the boy in the shop, Detective-Sergeant Monaghan and P.C. Barlow. A DISHONEST WATCHMAKER'S ASSISTANT. On Tuesday morning, at the Borough Police Court, before Mr. IL Garnett (chairman), Mr. E. J. Guest, and Dr. T. Starkey Smith, Patrick Edward Macdonald was charged with stealing from 31 Winwick-st., some time on Thursday, the 31st January, a silver lever watch, value £2 10s., the property of William Dodwell.—ln his statement to the magistrates, the Chief Constable stated that complainant, William Dodwell, was a watchmaker at the above address, and the defendant had been em- ployed at his shop. On Thursday last week a man named Adams left his watch to be repaired at the premises in question and on Friday called tor, and it was found to be missing. The defendant had not turned up to his work and on Monday the matter was reported to the police, and the same day Detective Monaghan saw the defendant in a public-house and called him out- side questioned him, and at length elicited that defend- ant 'had sold the watch for another and 4s. in cash. The stolen watch was produced and identified.—The magis- trates sent defendant to gaol for two montk—' ha" labour.

At the Borough Police Court on Monday morning before the Mayor (Councillor James Fairclough) chair- man, and other magistrates, James Leslie, 9 Orchard- street, was charged with stealing from the Patten Arms Hotel on Saturday the 2nd inst., a saucepan value 2s. 6d. the property of Mary Ellen Kiernan, landlady of the Patten Arms ; he was also charged with stealing from i the same place on the Ist of May last, a preserving pan value 10s.—Chief Constable aunt stated that defendant was a loiterer,and on Saturday night last about 6 o'clock Detective Sergeant Monaghan was coming down Church- street when ha met the prisoner with a saucepan upon his head. Monaghan asked him where he had got his new hat from and defendant said he got it from his sister's house. He was brought to the police station and , Monaghan made inquiries and found that the articles were missing from the Patten Arms. Frank Wilson, yard man, returned with Monaghan to the Police Station and identified the saucepan. In company ith Detec- tive Inspector Spinks, Monaghan went to prisoner's lodgings and found the preserving pan which prisoner's sister said he had brought on the first of May. Other evidence having been produced defendant was sent to gaol for one Month. THRFT OF A SACK OF FLOUR.

At the Borough Police Court on Tuesday morning be- fore Mr. R. Garnett and other magistrates, Charles Roberts was charged with stealing from the Mersey Mill, at 6.45 on Monday morning, a sack of flour value 203. the property of Messrs. Fairclough and Sons.—The de- fendant who appeared sorry for his misdeed pleaded guilty. —Mr. S. Hunt (chief constable), stated that the complainants were Messrs. Fairclough and Sons and the defendant was a carter for the firm. He had been in their employ for the last five years, and he resided at the Twelve Houses, Howley. On Tuesday Morning about 3 quarter to seven the defendant left the Mills with a load of flour for the Central Station, Warrington. He was seen while passing through Academy-st., to de- liver at a house there, a sack of flour which he had taken cff the cart in a suspicious manner. Information was given to Inspector Spinks, who went to the house in question, saw the sack, and communicated with the complainants. The bag was then identified. A ticket, which should have been on the bag had been wrenched off. As the defendant would have to pass that way backagain, Inspector Spinks waited, and on his appear- ance apprehended him and brought him to the Police Station, When charged there, the defendant denied the theft and afterwards said'' I will tell you the truth, I did take it." Defendant being a man of previous good character, the bench after a short consultation with Mr. R. T. Fairclough, who repr-sented the firm, said that though it was a serious offence they did not wish to deal unduly hard with defendant especially as be had a wife and seven children, but they could not pass the offence over, and therefore tined the defendant 403. in- cluding costs or one month's imprisonment.—The Chair- man afterwards added that it was to Mr. R. T. Fair- clone h that defendant was indebted for being dealt wilh so leniently. '• '

He admitted haying had the coat and =old it to a youth named James Whitehead for another coat and 3s, in cash.—Tl'e father of defendant had no doubt that he had also taken the toilet cover, but did not wish to press the case.—The -defendant had a precious bad character, and was sent to gaol for three months' hard labour. THEFT FROM A YARD.—George Gilligan. 3, Hughes-st., off Golborne-st.,was charged with stealing from the back- yard of William Gleave, 108, Wilderspool-road, at seven o'clock on Tuesday evening, a quantity of coal value 41. —The prisoner pleaded guilty. From the evidence it appeared that P.C. Barlow was, however, not satisfied and brought the prisoner down to the Police Station, , and afterwards going to Mrs. Gleave who denied giving ; the prisoner any coal. She had she said of late been I constantly missing quantities of coal.—This being pri- soner's first offence he was dismissed, but had a convic- tion recorded against him. , THURSDAY.—Before the Mayor (chairman) and Alderman

A FARM-HAND'S CLAIM. ry Hughes (youth) claimed £6 trom James Leigh, the balance of wages due to him from Ist January to 31st December 1894.—Mr. A. Browne represented the plaintiff, and stated that his client was hired by the year at Leigh's Doe Green Farm for £9 the year. Matters went on all right until the latter part of the year when Mr. Leigh was sold up by the bailiffs and the plaintiff left in November and had received up to that Maio £1 17s. 3d. When he left he asked defendant for payment but Mr. Leigh told him he had no money te pay him. They therefore claimed V. No attempt had been made to pay until the summons was served and since then they had received an offer from defendant hut could not accept it—Henry Hughes, living with Mr. John Owen, Station-road. Penketh, sup- ported what Mr. Browne had said.—The bench gave a verdict for £6 to the plaintiff with costa. T. Rigby. THE CHARGE OF CRITSLTY ' TO A DM—Julius Pick- atcck, Ellesmere-street, Runcorn, was again charged with having at Runcorn on the 10th September illtreated a dog by kicking the same. Mr. Burton, solicitor, re- presented the defendant. Mrs. Eliz Shallcross deposed that on the date named she was proceeding past Elles- mere-street accompanied by her dog when she met the. defendant who also had with him a fox terrier dog. The two animals commenced fighting, and she separated them. The defendant then kicked her dog, and it had suffered from the effects ever since. When she remon- strated with the defendant he used most abusive lan- guage and told her that he would treat her in the same way. In cross-examination she denied that the defen- dant kicked the dog to separate the animals. Annie Jones also gave evidence, but admitted that the dogs were fighting when the defendant kicked Mrs. Shall- cross's dog. Mr. Burton said there was no case for him to answer. The last witness had told them what took place. The defendant simply parted the two dogs. The magistrates dismissed the cam SCHOOL ATTENDANCB CASES.—Mr. T. Bowyer. school visitor, prosecuted in the following cases of irregular attend.% nce at school :—Tnomas Grestv, Wickstone Hill order issued for the child's attendance at school ; John Preston, Gas-street, and W.
