IWARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Warriugtnn Rural District Council was held on Wednesday afternoon, at the Bewsey Chambers, Bewsey-st. The Rev. G. F Roberts presided, and there were also present,Messrs. J.Dignem, T. Mather W. Houghton, J. Johnson, G. Thompson, J. W. Knowles. J. Ball, J. Warburton, J. Houghton, T. Halton, S. Sutton (clerk), W. Owen (surveyor), De. Sephton (medical officer), and F. Kerfoot (nuisance Inspector). Previous to the minutes being read. the Chairnmen expressed his pleasure at meeting in Bewsey Chambers, and expressed the opinion that it was far superior to the Workhouse. He hoped soon that the Board of Guardians and Committees would also be able to meet in some central building of the town. A LOW BALANCE IN HAND. The CLERK said that there was a balance in the hands of the treasurer of so low a sum as £5 13s. 11., and the general cheques to he met during the month were up- wards of £2O. Under these circumstances he must ask permission to write to the townships in arrears to pay up at once. Of course, they wauld receive the County Council payments some time in the month.—The neces- sary permission was OVSB. OUTBREAK OF SCARLET FEVER. The CLERK said that there had been an outbreak of scarlet fever at Poelton.with-Fearnhearl. He had received a letter from the schoolmaster at Padget asking what steps should be taken to arrest the epidemic. The schools had already been closed. He had also a communication from Mr.S.Brighouse,countv'coroner,enclosinga present- ment from a jury at an inquest at Poulton-with-Fearn- head upon a child who had died from scarlet fever. They requested that dm District Council be asked to take steps to arrest the epidemic. Dr. S*pht,nn sad that he bad not heard of an inquest previously. The doctor had not seen the deceased previous to her death. There were 19 cases of fever in the township.—The chairman said they oneht always to be prepared for emergencies in case of sudden outbreaks of epidemics of that kind.—lt was decided to reply to Mr Blackwell the schoolmaster, requesting him to report to the medical officer the sus- picious cases which came under his notice. THE PROPOSED FORT SANITARY AUTHORITY. A letter from the Town Clerk ef Manchester was read, addressed to the Council, and asking them whether as a riparian authority, they adhered to the decision of the late Rural, Sanitary Authority to join in with other riparian authorities along the banks of the Shin Canal to form a Port Sanitary Authority, and also inviting a de- Putation to attend a meeting to consider the suhject on Feb. 12.—1 t was decided to send a deputation consisting of the Chairman and Clerk to the meeting. COMPLAINT FROIE LITTLE SANKEY. The Clerk read a letter from Mr. R. B. Matthews, Chairman of Little Sankey Parish Council, complaining that the pavine of Gatewharf-q., Little Sankey,had not been completed, and wishing the Authority to go on with the work.—The Clerk said that the work ha ol not been gone on with because Messrs. (lreenall, Whitley and Co. ard Mr. Pusill, the owner of the property in the street, etapeted to pay for the paving nY the street, on the ground that it was a public highway, and, therefore, sh uld he eharged on the inhabitants at large. It had not been defieitelc settled whether this was !vs, but if it waa a highway, it would he a matter for the District ilighway Board It was decided to advise Mr. lat. thews to apply to the Highway Board.—Mr. Thompson also complained of a nuisanee at the Black Horse Inn, but was informed that it was a matter for the police.

_ THE EXTENSION OF.THE BOEOTIEH. A letter was read from the Clerk to the County Coun- cil stating that a representative from the County Couenil crifiald he /yegent when the inquiry wag held into th prorvwed extension of tha boundaeg of the horonch of W4rrinetm.—Mr. OWEN said that he had tinen offored a retainer in the application of the borough of Warriocton to extend the boundary, and he had aerAnteri it on .-he understandin7 that he would not he required ' o art, contrary to the interests of the Rural District C4tineil

RUNCORN V. ST. HELENS "A" TEAMS—This match was played on the Irwell-lane enclosure, Runcorn, on Satur- day, before a meagre attendance of spectators. Run- corn had only a poor team. The following were the contestants :—Runcorn : S. Booth, back; West,Myers, Nickson, and Dunvaband, tbreaquarter-backs ; Wood- ward and Clarke, half backs ; C. Pendlebury, Shaw, Peacock, Antrobus, Urmson, Reece, Thompson, and Ford, forwards. St. Helens : Pennington, full back ; Unsworth, Pritchard,Archer,and Gormelly, threequarter backs ; Harper and Wilson, half backs; Jones, Little, Fitz Gerald, Briers, Taylor, Dutton, Twist, and W. Pen- nington, forwards. Antrobus kicked off, and the open- ing stages were of a give and take character, end to end visits ensuing. Eventually Nickson started a dribble close from his own line, and steering the ball with ex- cellent judgment through his opponents, took the entire length of the field and scored underneath the posts, a grand individual performance. Dunvaband tailed at an easy place. From the restart Runcorn again pressed, ' West almost getting in after some pretty passing, Pen- I nington relieving his lines with the aid of a free kick. St. Helens now paid a visit to the other end, and Jones had a fine opening, but, a forward pass marred the , effort. The interval w,is reached with the score Run- corn one try, St. Helens nil. The second portion was very evenly touv,ht,although excellent efforts were made by Dunvaband and C. Pendlebury, the former getting over after a fine run, but an appeal for touch negatived the point. The final result was Runcorn one try, St Helens nil. RUNCORN V. Sr. HELENS.—On Saturday Runcorn journed to St. Helens to play the town club. Warder being unwell and W. Gayter being unable to play caused a re-arrangement of the team, but Mullineux, of the St. Helens Recreation, an old Runcornian, offered his ser- vices, and tho teams turned out as follows :—Runcorn : Jolley, full back ; Gregory, Butterworth, Houghton and , Mullineux, three-quarters • Abrams and J. Faulkner, halves; W. Faulkner, Taylor, F. Gayter, J. Langley, Farmer,Walker, Lightfoot and J. Pendlebury, forwards. St. Helens : Foulkes, back; Doherty, Appleton, Allen and Sudlow, three-quarters ' • Cross and McLees, halves; Brownbill, Gladwin, Briers, Rimmer. Graham, Whitely, Ashcroft and Dale,forwards. Cross kicked off, but there was no return. %V. Faulkner and Gregory, however, dribbled back to Cooke, whence Doherty punted back. J. Faulkner, Abrams, Houghton, Butterworth and Mul- lineux had an admirable sequence of passing, the latter putting to Foulkes, who failed to hold, and W. Faulkner caused a scrimmage in the home twenty-five. The ball was gradually worked out of danger. Brownbill, put in a very nice dribble, ;and being further supported by his confreres, a footing was got in the visitors' half. Some fine play was now witnessed in the Runcorn ranks, hand to hand passing by almost the whole of the team coming in for r considerable applause. Much ground was therefore gained. A free kick for offside play being awarded to Runcormfloughton tick it and further improved matters for the visitors. Immediately afterwards St. Helene had a free kick, but it gave them no advantage. Jolley again got a free catch and his return was well executed. The St. Helens' players now seemed to take a leaf out of the visitors' book, and Doherty receiving a pass from Cross quickly transferred to Sudlow,who was eventually held by Houghton. Half-time was called without any score being made. W. Faulkner restarted, and the ball was quickly rushed over, Foulkes kicking dead. Cross's drop out was splendidly returned by Houghton, and quick following up by Langley and Taylor put the home team on the defensive. A grand dribble by Briers gave relief, Gregory judiciously kicking into touch. A free kick to Runcorn caused the lost ground to be regained, which was in turn recovered by Allen having a free kick. Mullineux then dropped at goal,the home defence being sorely taxed, the ball being at length kicked dead. Following the drop out Abrams secured and almost got over, and in the next minute J. Faulkner dodged finely and secured a capital try. This infused life in the home forwards,and they came to centre in double quick time. Houghton, however, returned, and from the succeeding scrimmage Butterworth dropped a goal. Play continued to be of an open character, and now became located in the Rtincarn half. Jolley was taxed very heavily, but was full of resource and gener- ally found touch. St. Helens continued the attack, and Foulkes tried a drop at goal, which nearly came off, a minor resulting. W. Faulkner and Taylor followei up the drop out, and after a short scrimmage time was called, Runcorn winning a capitally contested game by one (dropped) goal, /me try, St. Helens nil. WIDNES " A " v. WARRINGTON ST. MARY'S.—Played at Widnes, on Saturday, before a poor gate and on a sodden ground. Elighfield started for Widnes, who were the first to attack, Corghan and Potter being con- spicuous with a run on the right. Tim visitors returned the pressure, and for a time the local goal was in jeopardy. Eventually a grand run by the forwards enabled Murphy to give Widnes the lead in the shape of a try. Even play followed, but the locals gradually got the upper hand and kept the visitors well penned in. Half-time—Widnes one try, Warrington nil. The second half was well contested, the visitors making some rushes, but the stout resistance offered by the home players neutralised all attempts to score. Peters made a grand run and secured a second try for Widnes, and this was converted by Highfield. The remainder of the game was fast and even, the visitors, if anything having slightly the best of matters. Final result Widnes" A," one goal one try ; Warrington St. Mary's nil. WARRINGTON RANGERS 2ND V. LATCRFORD RANGERS.— This match was played on the ground of the former,and a very even game resulted in a draw of two tries each.

PENKETH V. EARLESTOWN Vies—Played at Penketh on S l-tirday. The visitors, who only placed ten men,kicked off before a small " gate." The game had only been in progress a few minutes when Elliott received the ball on the right wing and put it across the goal mouth,andPar- son headed tho first gnal for Penketh. The Vies, took the hall down from the centre, one of their forwards sending in a splendid shot, which the Penketh goal keeper fisted over the line. Elliott now had a fine open- ing, hut he was pulled up for off-side, although he did not play the ball, Nit he left it to his partner Bowyer. The Vies, were awarded a free kick. Half time arrived in favour of Penketh—one goal to nil. Play was resumed at once. Each goal was visited in turn, the Vies. trying hard to equalise, forcing two successive corners. The Penketh goalkeeper now effected a brilliant save when a goal seemed certain. The homesters came away, and Penketh nere awarded a free kick. Dumbell took the kick, and Bowyer headed through and scored No. 2. Penketh finally ran out winners he three goals to nil. WARRINGTON ST. ELPHINS' V. OUGHTRINGTON PARK.— This' match was played at Dalton Rank, on Saturday, before a moderate number of spectators. Oughtrington started, and immediately went for the home team goal, hut were cleared out by A. Duckworth. The home team took up the running, and had a shot at goal, which was unsuccessful. Not to he denied, the home team worked the ball up the field, and DAndy scored with a good shot. Immediately after the restart the visitors equalized through a miskick by one of the home backs. This put fresh life into the Saints, and J. Duckworh getting pos- session raced away, and passing well out to Hatton,that Player scored. The Saints put on six more goals through J. Duckworth (four), Dandy (one), and Hickinbottom (one), and run out winners by eight goals to one. WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT AMATEUR LEAGUE. I Results up to Saturday last FLINT Dimwit.

THE IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. OPENING ON TUESDAY. The fourth session of the thirteenth Parliament of Her Majesty Queen Victoria was opened on Tuesday by Royal Commission. The Speech from the Throne was read by the Lord Chancellor. It spoke of our continued friendly relations with foreign powers, said that no favourable+ opportunity of promoting a peaceful termena- tion of4the conflict between China and Japan would be lost, and referred to the appointment of the Armenian Commission. Satisfaction was expressed at the orderly condition of Ireland, and a bill promised dealing with . .

the land question in_, that cotmtry. The other leading measures to be brought forward were stated in the following order :—The Welsh Church Bill, Liquor Traffic Bill, Bills for the Abolition of Plural Voting and the Pay- ment of Returning. Officers' Charges, Construction .of

Light Railways Bill, a Trade Disputes Conciliation Bill, and a Factory Acts Amendment Bill. In the House of Lords the Address was moved by Lord Welby and seconded by Lord Battersea. The Marquis ,of Salisbury said there was a very remarkable omission in the Speech. They had heard that a revolution of a most portentous kind was intended. If they had a revolution on their programme it ought to come first on the list. In all the Government did there was a double- ness which implied either that there were two leaders or that the single leader ss as a man of singularly change- able mind. The Prime Minister, in reply,said he was at a loss to know on what precedent the noble Marquis based himself in anticipating that a paragraph in the

Queen's Speech would announce a resr:Autkin Which at some time or other was to be introduced into the House of Commons with reference te the relations of the two Houses. It would be an act of disrespect in the first and highest degree to the House into which jt was to be introduced if they were to anticipate the introduc- tion of the resolution in the House of Commons by even describing it •in the House of Lords. Be (Lord Rosebery) asked the members of that House to divest their minds of the impression that the introduc- tions of the various bills would be mere acts in a drama and that thee were not meant for serious consideration, but merely for debate in the House of Commons and then to be flung out by that House in August. The idea of the Government was to give an honest fulfilment to the pledges they gave in Opposition. After some re- marks by the Duke of Devonshire, the Address was agreed to, and the House adjourned. The first business of the House of Commons was the swearing-in of the new members. When Mr. Broad- hurst, one of the members for Leicester, advanced to the table, Sir 11. JAMES asked permission to" raise a question," but the SPEAKER said he could allow no in- terference between a member and his taking his seat. At the close of the formalities Sir H. JAMES questioned the validity of the return of Mr. Broadhurst and Mr. Hazel!, for Leicester, and asked the Chanceilor of the Exchequer whether there was any objection to the mat- ter being referred to a Committee. Sir W. Harcourt said he should be happy to agree to the course suggested,and Sir H. James gave notice that on Thursday or Friday he would make a motion on the subject. Ministers gave notice, in the order here named, of their intention to ask leave on Thursday to bring in the following mea- sures :—Welsh Disestablishment Bill, Irish Land Bill, Local Veto Bill , Light Railways Bill, Scotch County Government Bill, and a bill to prohibit plural voting at Parliamentary elections and to provide for taking the polls at Parliamentary elections on one day. The Address reply to the Queen's Speech was moved by Mr. C. Hob- house and seconded by Mr.. Holland.—.-Mr. Balfour, _

referring to the paragraPhs in the Queen's Speech did not think that the diminution of offences in Ireland could btaclaimed !.,o be due to the policy of clemency pursued by the Chief Secretary. It was the culmina- tion of a continuous process dating back for eight or ten years, and was due to more deep-seated causes than hon. gentlemen seemed to think. Agricultural depres- sion in this country was now reaching the rank of a national traeedy, and the Government would receive from the Opposition all the assistance they could give in the matter ; hot he held that the construction of light railways ought not to involve cost to the ratepayers. As to the paragraphs dealing with the Government's legis lative programme, they were a farce, and were known to be a farce by those who proposed them. It seemed to him that a greater step towards the degradation of Parliament had never been taken than that which the Government new took. They had called members to- gether not to pass laws but to further some obscure strategic party purpose. Never had a Government at- tempted such revolutionary measures upon so small a capital, and he trusted that some member of autho- rity would move an amendment by which the House would have an opportunity of recording its judgment upon the subject. Sir W. Harcourt, after paying a tribute to the great influence exercised by the late Czar on the preservation of peace, said it was a melancholy reflection that while every ruler and Government in Europe ardently desired peace we should be called upon to be armed to the teeth as if we were in the presence of an instant and universal war. He agreed with the opinion of Count Kalnoky that this was due to the conduct of mischievous and ir- responsible persons who took upon themselves to sow dissension and jealousy. The Government were, he said, carrying out the naval proposals loyally and fully Passing on to Ireland, the right hen, gentleman said they maintained the establishment of Home RUl9as their primary policy. Whether there was to be one or two Bills on the land question, all he could say at pre- sent was that the Government reserved their discretion in the matter. He could not go into the flnancial ar- rangements about the light railways without anticipat- ing what would have to be said by Mr. Bryce. With regard to the legislative programme of the Government, Mr. Balfour's position was that no Government might to produce any measure which it did not know before- hand would be passed by the House of Lords. Let the House and the country mark that. The Government awaited the revelations on the right hon. gentleman's amendment with as much curiosity-as he (Mr. Balfour) felt about their revelations. They intended to pursue the measures to which they were pledged until the House of Commons had pronounced condemnation upon them. Mr. Justin M'Ca.rthy appealed to the Government to repeal the Coercion Act and to release this Irish political prisoners. Something should also be done for the labourers of Ireland. Mr. Vincent moved an amend- ment declaring that steps should be taken to remove any obstacles standing in the way of a Cristame Union ' between the different parts of the' United Kingdom. Mr. Godson seconded the amendment' After a few words from Mr. Buxton the amendment was withdrawn, and at midnight the debate on the Address was adjourned. WEDNESDAY.

When the House of Commons met on Wednesday Mr. SEXTON asked the CHIEF SECRETARY for Ireland whether he had any statement to make with reference to the state of primary education in Ireland. Mr. MORLEY replied that the Compulsory Education Act of 1892, which came into operation on the let of January, 1894, had really not been in force in many places, in some cases owing to Ow refusal of the local authorities to put it into operation so long as certain classes of schools were excluded from participation in the grants, and in others owing to lack of funds. The defects and oversights of that Act he in- tended to remedy by introducine as soon as possible the amending bill which he laid before the HOUSE last year. The debate on the Address was resumed by Sir E. A. BARTLETT, who complained that the Government had abandoned the Swazis to the ill-treatment of the Boers, and had also neelected to take steps to ensure the better treatment of English subjects in the Transvaal by the I Boers. He moved an amendment to the Address RE- pressing regret at the neglect of the Government to call attention in the Speech to the injustice with which British subjects in the Transvaal are treated by the Boer Government, and to the abandonment of the Claims of our Swazi allies to independence and security. The a mendrident was afterwards withdrawn. Mr. JEFFREYS then moved an amendment expressing apprehension at the disastrous condition of the agricultural intere t, the prolonged depression of the textile and other industries, and the consequent increase of the number of the un- employed, and regret that the Government had not shown their appreciation of the extreme gravity of the present situation. Mr. WHARTON seconded the amend- ment.. The debate was continued by Mr. CHARRING, and on the motion of Mr. CHAPLIN it was adjourned. WELDON'S LADIES' JOURNAL February (3d). This popular magazine is nothing if not up-to-date, per lady readers may rely on being well posted with the latest of fashion fancies, and will fully appreciate the current issue of this widely circulated monthly. A large coloured plate is•presented of seasonable fashions, also two paper Patterns of tweed knicker-bockers and gaiters. The sub- ject of sensible underwear was fully discussed in the previous iSSIIe and so greatly appreciated, that the paper pattern of gaiters and the improved knickers tor ladies are now given away, these knickers are intended to re- place the flannel petticoat thus affording full freedom to the limbs. The issue contains the usual clear and prac- tical directions for cutting out and making up at home, ; all the latest fashion creations for ladies and children I There are some useful articles on household management fancy work, cookery, home dressmaking and millinery, an excellent number in everyway and a marvel of cheapness and utility.

. ANNUAL MEETING. The annual meeting of the Warrington Climber of Commerce was held on Monday afternoon at the office of thu Secretary, Market Gate Chambers. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. H. Fleming, J.P., and there were also present, Messrs. William Pierpoint, J.P., Garnett, J.P., J. Fairclough, J.P., and A. Bennett (secretary).

SECRETARY'S REPORT. The eighteenth annual report was submitted by the secretary. It stated that the year had been one of con- tinueus activity. ,Twice a year the Associated Chambers of Commerce of the united Kingdom met in conference, once in London, and once in the provinces. Mr. Wllljurn Long attended the last London meeting on behalf of the Warrington Chamber, and reported that the executive' were actively engaged in furthering the commercial Me terests of the empire ; that their representations received the most careful considerations of the Government that the deliberations of the delegates were exceedinelf interesting and important in their bearing on the con)" mercial questions of the day. The Council were invited by the labour department of the Social Questions IfnioP to appoint a deputation to meet deputations from the. Union and from the Warrington Trades and Labour Council, in order that the qhrestion of forming a Board of Conciliation :night be reconsidered, and a solution, it possible, arrived at. The secretary was instructed tu'' reply that the Council thought it wiser to defer any fur; ther action until it was seep what shape the propoeKt' legislation upon the subject would ul:imately take. Cer— tificates of origin on goods exported to foreign countriee might now be obtained at the offiees of the Chamberesed the Council were pleased to find, as they expected,that the facilities thus afforded had proved a great conveni- ence to local manufacturers. A comprehensive schema' of commercial education was submitted by the London Chamber, but the Council considered that the Warring- ton Technical Institute sufficiently satisfieJ the require' meats of the town in the matter. Councillor Mos" having called the attention of the Commit to the .repon*, that although the P. and 0. Steamship Company we° subsidized by the Imperial Government. they carried foreign goods at lower rates than British, the Counci communicated with the Board of Trade upon the sue ject, and received through them, a letter, which wig subsequently published in the local papers to the eff that although the Compiny were entirely in accord with the feeling of the Chametr that freights from continental ports should be at least as high as from British ports,ell,l would indeed prefer that they should he higher, and bee done their best for a long series of years to give effecc to this principle, the subsidy they received was not sofa' cient to enable them to decline to, accept whatorre rates they were able to obtain. The Chamber was ill vited to assist in the establishment of an industrial union of employers and employed, the object of which wo to obviate strikes and lock-outs, and in various other ways to promote a better understanding between capital and labour. The secretary was instructed to exPresi/ the sympathy of the Council with the objects of the Union. The question of railway rates was several timeS under consideration, and the Council did what teel could to suppoet the Mansion House Aesociation on rail- way and canal traffic in their endeavours to remove tbe misting anomalies which pressed so heavily upon Britisb trade. In order that members of Chamber might obtain assistance in disputes with railway companies, it bad been arranged to affiliate with the Mansion [louse AS ation. A suggestion of Mr. John Fairclooeh that the mercantile marine and naval services should be largelY recruited from workhouse and industrial schools, W 5 adopted :at the autuirmal meeting of the Aseociate° Chambers.

A resolution was passed at the , annual meeting in February, pledging the Chamber to , support the Corporation by every means in, their power ' in safeguarding the interests of the borough, and ia obtaining frons the Ship Canal Company the privilege* to which it was entitled. THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WARRING-TON.

A very interesting discussion took place on Satur- day evening, last week, at the quarterly meeting of the P.S.A. Federation upon "Char- acter in public life." Councillor Park, of Ashton-under-Lyne, opened the discussion and many leading men from other: towns took part in it. Councillor 'Jiggle, of Rochdale, rather surprised his hearers by telling them th at in Rochdale there was a political club which flourished and yet there was no drink sold in it. This is rather an eye-opener. It was generally agreed by the various speakers that the P.S.A. societies should be kept as free as possible t rom political influences. An interesting announcement by the Rev. J. Yonge WAS that the Social Questions Union was still alive, and would come to the front whenever occasion re- quired it.

--- The "Fireman " has during the past two and a half years given a seric.s of short sketches of the " British Fire Chiefs (Past. and Present)," being an account of the work of the various superintendents of the fire brigades of Great Britain. In the current issue of February, it deals with the Warrington fire brigade of the past history of which some very interesting information is given. It appears that the earliest record of a fire in Warrington is one in August 1791, although there were no doubt many fires previously. It is supposed that some kind of a fire brigade existed a 5 that time, but nothing definite is known until 1828, when there were six manual engines. Mr. John Smith appears to have been the first chief superintendent of the Warring- ton fire brigade, and in 1839, a 9in, and a 7iti. manual engine was obtained, and named " Victoria " and the " Duke," which latter is still in good working order. Mr. Smith died in 1844.

The superintendent at the time of the incorpora- tion of the borough was Mr. W. butt, but soon after the incorporation it was thought desirable to incorporate the fire engine department with the police under the command of Captain Charles Stewart. Police arrangement did not work well however, and in 1850 Mr. James Woods was ap- pointed separate superintendent of the fire brigade. lie held this post until 1879, having attended during his term of office 230 fires, including Allen's factory Buttermarket-st., and Cockhedge factory. atter Mr. Woods' resignation there were several Inanges, up to October sth, 1882, when Mr. Prank Turner took the position, there having been no fewer than three inspectors or superintendents, viz., Mr. Matthew Chorley, Inspector John Proffitt, and Mr. R. Spann.

The present superintendent as every one knows is Mr. Frank Turner, who has been connected with the brigade since 1861, except for a very brief in- terval. "During his long connection with the brigade Mr. Turner has had one or two narrow escapes of losing his life. On July 31st, 1874, at a fire in the Liverpool Road Size and Glue Works the walls collapsed while he was playing with a branch inside the building, he being taken from under a large beam apparently lifeless, his helmet being crushed over his face. He was, however, only in- sensible, and he recovered in about two hours. At a fire at Bewsey Farm, the same year, the walls again fell, and he was buried under them. He was, however, got out unhurt. This made him very cautious,. and on November 26th, 1878, at the Wharf Meadow Factory, which was completely gutted, he was instrumental in saving the lives of four of his comrades who were playing inside the upper room of the building. The rooms underneath were burning fiercely. Seeing their dangerous position he ordered them below; they had just cleared the building when the old structure crashed to the ground." The journal pay a high compli- ment to the manner in which Mr. Turner has super- intended the brigade.

The Photographic Society held its annual meeting on Tuesday evening, last week, but the majority of members were not enthusiastic enough to brave the severe weather which was experienced on that day. Consequent- ly the election of officers was postponed until a more representative meeting was held. The Secretary, Mr. Pritchard, had a report to give which was satisfactory as far as it went,but he had again to deplore, as he had often done before, that the members would not attend in larger numbers at the monthly meeting. With this exception, a satisfactory report was given, for there is a good membership, and the society is also gaining in "property." It has often been said that the Gymnasium is no such a success as it might be—and no doubt there is some reason forthe statement—but it could not possibly be said.with truth,that the gymnaastic dis- play:on Tuesday evening, last week, for the benefit of the worthy conductor, was anything but the acme of success. To commence with there was an exceedingly large attend- ance, and then the ladies took a large share in the performances, and lain sure that a great number of those present were surprised at the excellence in all departments attained by the fair sex. Their forte was in the drills—dumb-bell and clubs—when the rhythmical regularity, 80 dear to an onlooker versed in calisthenicQ,which characterized the exer- cises, excited unbounded admiration especially as the ladies themselves looked extremely pretty in their neat blue and white costumes. It was in the tug of war—girls v. boys—that the natural order of things was reversed in an amusing and, shall I say, rather alarming manner, by the unexpected tri- umph of the hitherto weaker sex over the stronger. Reath, there is no getting over the fact that a new era is coming, when the ladies not content with entering the world's strife, coolly outdo their " masters" in muscular power, certainly, at this rate, their description as of " better halves "will not be without a substantial justification. Still, it is hardly likely that any precocious female will ever emulate, the muscular dexterity evinced by the men on the rings, parallel, and horizontal bars, for some of the teats performed, seemed to threaten immediate dislocation of a limb or two. The box- ing contest between Fair Turner and Harry Ashton was undoubtedly responsible for a large part of the attendance, as such an exhibition has not often been witnessed in Warrington of late years. Both men were " fit " and their dexterity with the gloves was roundly applauded.

div.head: WARRINGTON DEBATING SOCIETY AND THE
div.p: WARRINGTON DEBATING SOCIETY AND THE
I.L.P.

Sir,—My letter on the above subject was written at the request of the Executive of the Party, to correct an erroneous statement which appeared in your paper and to point out the true cause of the interruptions. I have neither cause nor desire to personally attack Mr. Horton, and I am sorry he has constrged my letter as such ; bat I mast say, the implication contained in the state- ment that I " presumably " wrote at the wish of the Executive Is, to say at least, ungentlemanly. He says ke respects any party. I accept that statement, only suggesting that he shows his respect a little more in future than he did on the occasion under discussion. I notice he makes a wrong statement and a misquotation. I did not state" the I.L.P. were led on to interrupt by their Socialist friends," for the first to interrupt were not Socialists, neither did our two speakers " lecture " us. I have nor wish to pursue this matter further, but I would suggest this question for Mr. Horton's quiet study. " What is the workers' honest share of the wealth his labour produces ? " Ho may find an answer in " Merrie England."—Yours, etc., .1. PODMORE, jun. P.S.—The I.L.P. is a " family " of Socialists gathered from every ward in the town ; who when they need advice may apply to someone perhaps better qualified to give it, than Mr. Horton.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday at the Workhouse, when the chair wAs oc- cupied by Mr. W. Houghton. There were alio present. Mrs. Clay, Rev. J. H. Riddette, Messrs. S. thyies, G. Piling, d. Billiage, J. Clarke, J. Dignuin, W. Cross, T Halton, W. Hickman, H. Hibbert, A. dolley,A. J. Jolley, A. Lang, T. B. Malkin, G. Thompson, J Warburton,Dr. Patterson, J. Ball, J. W. Knowles, J. Johnson, E. L. Beat, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (deputy clerk), C. H. Ward (ouster), and El. M. Mines (superintendent). HMI CONIXITTIIII. Ths House Committee recommended that the offer of Miss Hulme to visit patients at the hospital be declined. They also reeonsmended that the names of Miss Massey and Mrs. John Fairclough be added to the Ladies' Committals. Also that an assistant matron be appointed to assist Mrs. Ward. The committee declined to adept tbe medical officer's recommendation that he be sent for in all lying in cases, and only recommended that he be sent for in cases of urgeut character. They recommended that a tender be obtained so supply 190 blankets.—Mr. Davies moved, and Mr. Billings seconded the adoption of the minuteo.—The Rev. J. H. ftiddette moved that the sub- ject of an additional matron be referred back to the House Committee. Having regard to the proposed new infirmary it was well that the question be left is abey- ance. He did not wish to say anything in hostility to the matron, as he believed her to be a zealous and inde- fatigable officer deserving of the best support olthe Board. It would, however, be extremely unwise to make aay additional appointment until it had been settled with regard te the new infiriwary.—Mr. Clarke seconded the amendment.—The Clerk pointed out that the matter would eome up for consideration at the tout meeting, and Mr.Riddetts then withdrew his amendment,and the minutes were carried—Mr. Billinge gave notice that at the next meeting he would move the appointment of a head nurse who should have full charge of the nurses sad patients in the infirmary. APPLICATIONS FOR RELIEF. Th, Cthax said that the Local Government Board were desirous of being informed whether there had been during the recent winter months, any material Increase In the number of applications for relief as compared with that of corresponding weeks is previoua two or three years.—The Clerk said that last year the coal strike tools place and there was much relief given by private per- sons. The reply sent to the Local Government Board was as follows. In December and Ltnuary 18,2-3, the number of applications for relief was 752, 1893 4, 675 1394-s,793.—Mr.Davies said that there was a good no mb• er of people out of work through the had weather. He was sorry that there was no agency whereby a:sistance could he given without applying to the Bard. He under- stood that there was something left of the fund from last year, and he thought the present time was the right time to use it.—Mr. Clay said that relief was now being distributed at the Town Hall. MilFoftlf TINATMBNT OF C1,17AL5.

The Decal Government Board have issued representa- tion to Boards of Guardians recommending that uniform treatment be meted out to casuals. The Clerk said that he believed that uniform treatment should be used— Mr. Thompson asked whether the casuals were given anything to eat on Sunday morning on leaving the BOUM), and if so what did they get.—Mr. Curry, who was called in, said that they received eight ounce.; Of bread and some water. They had no ' butter.—Mr Thompson, I should not like the uniform treatment of casuals to be like Warrington.—Mr. Lang thought that more precautions should tie taken to prevent the mixing of casuals with the rest of the inmates of the House.— Mr. Ward said that they were kent separate. PROPOSED CENTRAL BUILDINGS FOR THB mama. The CLERIC said that in Sankey-st., the Warrington Corporation had acquired some property adjoining the Town Hall, formerly occupied by Dr. Soinks. He be- lieved that the Corporation would favourably coniider an application from the Guardians to t-,lre this building as offices. It was in a desirable situation between the stations and in the centre of the town.—lt was decided to form a committee cougisting of Messrs.Davies,Pillin,g, A. J. Jolley, and Hickman• to wait upon the Town Clerk upon the subject. RI,MOVAL OF THI4 ICHWTON RELINE OFFICE. Mr. CLARKS moved the adoption of recommendation of the Newton Relief Committee to remove the office from Newton to the Town Doll, EITIrStOWiI, at a rental of £1.4 per annuns.—Mr. Billinge seconded, and said that the greater number of people who required tresided in Earlestown, and formerly, the people had to walk 21'i miles to the Newton oflice.—Mr. Hibbert strongly opposed the proposed alteration,and Dr. Patter- son supported it, and the recommendation was adopted. COMPLAINTS CONCHRNING TRBATAISNT OF PATIENTS. Mr. THOMPSON said that there had been a number of complaints with regard to the treatment of the inmates in the infirmary. He suggested that in the interests of the officers themselves, it would be well tliat a small committee, say of three, should be appointedoto go to the infirmary at a time privately fixed by themelves, and question the patients. They could then give an authoritative statement to the public on the matter.— Mr. Dignum and the Chairman pointed out that any member of the Board could visit the House at any time, and that therefore Mr. Thompson's object could be gained by arranging with one or two members of the Board.

- A THLL-TALE CLOCK. Mr. Tnoursos brought a tell-tale clot* for the in- spection of the Board. He said that he had no feeling in the matter, but if they were desirous of having one, the one he produced was one of the best.—Mr. Billingo could not see the utility of having such a thing. He thought-that they should not use one unless they hid cause to distrust their officers. This concluded the business of the Board.

div.head: WESTON.
div.p: WESTON.
NEW TALE! • NEW TALE!!

Tna Da T ScHoot PRIZR Fusn.—A concert was given ; in the Church schools, Weston, on Monday evening, the proceeds of which were in aid of the Day School Prize Fund. The Rev. Canon Maitland Wend, M.A ,presided. A programme of songs, duets, glees, &c., was given by the children, and a number of infant scholars gave seve- ral drills. Recitations were contributed by W.Robinson J. Pickering, M. Jones, and G. Moores. The following gave songs :—H. Milward, M. Owen, G. Bankes, F. Howard, J. H. Bankes, J. Hardman, Miss Wale, and Messrs. J. E. Tudor, and J. Williams. A duet entitled, " Where are you going ?" was rendered by L.Tudor and Stanley Orme. Messrs. W. and J. E.Tudor performed a cornet duet.

the explanation, but he would ask the Law Clerk NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL!I whether the Surveyor had always to be instructed in his ection,where bye-laws were laid down. His opinion. was that Mr. Brierley was in order in issuing the notice —Mr. Emmett hardly thought that Mr. Brierley was in order by putting the Councils' name to it, when the Ihing had never been discussed or named at the Council. —Mr. Simpson said if Mr. Emmett was at the last meet- ing he would have had the matter brought forward.— Ms. Gilmour: I say no I—Mr. Simpson: I say yes ; it was decided that Mr. Brierley should issue that notice to the public.—The Chairman thought they had gone quite far enough over that small matter. The Law Clerk had advised Mr.Brierley that he was quite in order in issuing the notice, without bringing it before the Council. The time of the Council had been wasted over such a small affair.—Mr. Evans asked whose duty it was to keep the footpath from Mercer-street to the Mesnes in order.— Mr. Ormand said that was a question which stood in his name. The question was that the Law Clerk be asked as to the maintenance and repair of public footpaths.— The Chairman said no additional powers had been granted by the 1894 Act, than what the Commissioners had previously. He did not know that he was prepared to say that all footpaths were kept in repair by the Council or by the owners of property adjoining.—Mr. Emmett understood the footpath was diverted, and he asked was it in good order before the diversion. He did. not see that Lord Newton should be allowed to get out of keeping the footpath in repair.—The Chairman thought they were all agreed that it was their duty to look after footpaths, and they would in future do so. The Law Clerk would look further into the question raised by Mr. Ormand.—Mr. Smith said it would be better if notice was given of these questions.—Mr. Orraand said Mr. Smith was not in order, the question had been standing in his name for some time.—The minutes were then passed.—The minutes of the special committee were also passed on the motion of Mr. Collingwood seconded by Mr. Thompson.

The monthly meeting of the Urban District Council of Newton-in-Makerfield was held at the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Monday evening. Mr. C. B. F. Borron presided, and the other members present were Messrs. W. Collingwood. J. W. Emmett, J.P., R. Stone. J.P., T. Ormand, F. J. Wood. P. McMahon, E. T. Evans, J. Simpson, W. Gilmour W. Beatty, W. Thompson, jun., and Jimes Smith, IP. ;J. E. Woreley (law clerk), R. Brierley (clerk and surveyor). Dr. Watkins, medical officer was also preset.
&dim
GAS AND WATER.

At a tneetingef thecoaTa—nci—Vl-a-t-e; Committee hold on the 21st January, the carbonising account for the past month was read. It showed fuel used 480 tons, gas made 4,825,300 feet, being an average ef 10,043 feet per ton of fuel used. The Gas Manager's report was read giving the illurainating power of the gas ranging from 1826 candles. One hundred and thirty protection meters had now been fixed at a cost of about £292. The gas and water mains over Newton Common have been broken again during the past month, owing to subsi- dence, and causing serious loss, of both gas and water. The water supply to the gas works since August last was 305,000 gallons. The manager asked for more covered accommodation for storing fuel, and preparations for ground for turning over the oxide of iron. The report was adopted by the meeting. Resolved that the representatives of each ward report what further public lamps they consider necessary in their respective wards.—Mr. Borron moved and Mr. Stone seconded the adoption of the minutes.— Mr. Emmett asked if any claim had been made upon the party who had caused the subsidence by which the gas and water pipes had been broken.—The Chairman said from the reports he had of former years there had been a continuance of breakages in Crow-lane on ac- count of the mining operations there, and no doubt the Clerk would be able to tell them what proceedings were taken at that time.—The Clerk said no proceedings whatever had been taken; the Commissioners simply re- paired them.—The Law Clerk was instructed to go int* the question and advise the Council.—The minutes were then passed.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
POLICE CEANGES.

P.C. Twaddle has -been t;:a-n-sie-r-r-e'd from Earlestown to the Leyland division, the vacancy being filled by P.C. Turner of Birkdale. A SUCCESSFUL MEDICAL STUDENT. At an examination of the Pharmaceuticial Society held in Liverpool at the beginning of January, Mr. W. H. Owen, son of Mr. Charles Owen, of the Royal Hotel, and sit apprentice of Mr. Peake was successful in passing as a Chemist and Dentist.

DRUNKEINNESS. At the Town Hall, Newton, before Mr. T. 3. Gillespie and Colonel Wood, on Monday morning, Blandina Bar- nett, of Legh-st., Earlestown, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Ashton Read, on Saturday night, was fined 51. and costs. Sent to gaol for 14 days in default.—Samuel Baker, of Mercer-st., Newton, for being drunk and disorderly in High-st., Newton, on Saturday night, was fined 21. C. and costs.—Patrick Naughten, of Legh-et., Earlestowa, for being drunk and disorderly in Tamworth-st., on Saturday night, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.

TBMPARANCE ENTBSTAINMENT AT ELELBSTOWN. An entertainment was given in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, on Saturday night, under the auspices of the Hope of Earlostown lodge of Good Templars. Mr. G. Dring presided, and an interesting address was given by Bro. Morris Jones, D.Sec. of Liverpool. A good pro- gramme of instrumental pieces, songs recitations, &c., was given by Messrs. W. Willis, J. fluddleston, F.Wlaar- mough, W.Wilson, W. H. Crowther, A. Haynes, Misses .T. Roberts, R. Warburton, and Jackson, and Mr. G. Clarke gave a" Lancashire reading." SONS OF TEMPBRANCS. In connection with the Samuel Morley section of Cadets of Temperance No. 219, an entertainment was given in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, on Wednesday even- ing. Bro. A. Chalmers, of Haydock, presided, and there was a fair audience. A couple of songs were given by Sisters E. L. Collinge and 0. Clare, and recita- tions by Bros. A. Wilkinson, and Arnold Clare, and Sis- ter .1. Pickett. The chief portion of the entertainment consisted of exhibitions of sleight of hand tricks, which were both clever and amusing, the " Necromancer " be- ing Bro. B. Teighlor, who was frequently applauded. During the evoping prizes were distributed to Janet Pickett, Ethel Pearson, and Amy Clare, for having brought in the greatest number of members to the order.

GOOD TEMPLABY., The weekly session of the Elope of Earlestown Lodge ef Good Templars was held in the Co-operative Hall, Barlestown. on Monday evening. Bro. Joseph Anderton P.C.T., presided, and there was a large attendance of members. Representatives for No. 1 Convention and for the District lodge were elected. On the motion of Bro. Blair, seconded by Bro. J. Halton, it was resolved to forward a letter of condolence to Sister Broster on the death of her husband. Bro. G. Clarke, sec., presented his quarterly report which was of a very satisfactory character, showing an increase of membership,the num- ber on the books being 157. The financial statement was presented by Bra. J. T. Holliday, F. See. The re- ports were adopted. The isfficers for the ensuing quarter were then installed by Sister J. H. Warburton, L.D.,' as- sisted by Q.M. Sergeant Roberts, and Sister R. Cord- ingly, who acted as Marshalls, as follows :—C.T., Bro. J. Miller ; V.T., Sister M. Eaton ; Sec. Bro. B. Barker; F.Sec.,Bro. J. H. Williams; Treas., Bro. T. Pope ; chap.. Bro. W. Wainwright ; M., Bro. A. E. Dale. The Sick and Finance Committees were afterwards appointed. SAD SHATINO FATALITY AT NSWTON LAIL On Monday morning about ten o'clock, a lad named James Thomas Brown, 14 years of age, son of a signal- man residing in Golborne Dale Road, Golborne, lost his life while skating on Newton lake. The lad left home about nine o'clock in company with two other lads, James Cook and Adam Mather, for the purpose of skat- ing on Newton lake. On arrival there, they put on their skates and commenced skating, the deceased going on the ice first. When he got into the middle of the lake, opposite the landing stage, the ice suddenly gave way, and be fell into the water, which at that point was about 18 feet deep. Cook was a little behind him, but managed to turn aside and escaped. The deceased came to the surface three times and then sank, no assistance being rendered, as the ice was only a quarter of an inch thick. Information was given to Inspector Morgan and Sergeant Longworth, who stance went with three con- stables and got a long ladder and tried te put it over the shOle, but ths ice was so thin that it would not hold. A boat was then procured from Lord Newton's yard and grappling commenced. and the body was recovered by Mr. J. Barrow and PC. Green, at 12.15. The body was removed to a friend's house in Mercer-st., and efforts to restore animation were resorted to, but without success. The inquest on the body of the deceased lad was held at the Blue Lion Inn, Newton, on Wednesday morning by Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner. Evidence of identification was given by Thomas Brown, signalman, father of the deceased. Geoffry Barrow, lakekeeper, also tendered evidence of the finding of the body, and stated that on Sunday he had several times driver' lads away from the ice, and notices were posted warning people that the ice was dangerous.—James Cook, who was with deceased on the ice, and Sergeant Longworth also gave evidence, and the jury returned a verdict of accidentally dr mned. ALARMING BOILNII EXPLOSION AT EARLEISTOWN. On Wednesday afternoon the residents of Bridge-st., Eirlestown, and the neighbourhood adjoining were alarmed by a loud explosion, which on inquiry wag found to originate in a large unoccupied shop at the corner of King and Bridge-streets, belonging to Mr. C. Birchall, of Liverpool. The shop is one of a block of five recently erected, and has only just been completed, bet has not yet been tenanted. The shop is fitted with a bath with hot and cold water on the circulating prin. ciple,the boiler being situated at the back of the kitchen fire. For two or three days past a fire has been lighted, in order to air the place, but during Tuesday night it had gone out, and it is supposed that the severe frost had frozen the water in the pipes. On Wednesday morn- ing the fire was re-lighted, no suspicion of anything wrong being entertained. Shortly before three o'clock in the afternoon, however, a terrific explosion took place, and extensive damage was caused. It was found that the iron boiler had burst and completely wrecked the fireplace, blown. the kitchen window out bodily for some distance, torn off the kitchen door, and completely demolished the two large plate glass windows at the front of the shop. A. portion of thn boiler was found in King-st. some distance away. Fortunately there was nobody about at the time, and thus no person was in- jured. The damage is roughly estimated at about 240.

The Law Clerk having read the minutes of the last meeting, Mr. Ormand said there was some little con- fusion in them with regard to the appointment of chair- man of the School Attendance and Technical Instruction Committees.—Mr. Emmett said there was also another slight mistake; Mr. Ratcliffe objected to be chairman of the Highway Committee.—Mr. Ormand painted out ' that Mr. Collingwood was unanimously appointed chair- man of the Technical Instruction Committee, and Mr. Wood was unanimously appointed chairman of the School Attendance Committee, and the Law Clerk seemed, in the minutes, to have infused the two appoint- ments into one.—After the minutes had been corrected, Mr. Ormand asked if the Law Clerk was creating a precedent, for on the occasion of his being appointed chairman of the Finance Committee, he (the law clerk) said that caused a vacancy. The very fact of his being appointed chairman of the Finance Committee, did not cause a vacancy; he simply refused to hold two offices, and he moved that Mr. Wood be appointed chairman of the School Attendance Committee. It was very import- ant that they had the minutes right at the first Council meeting.—lt was agreed to delete the words " vacancy " from the minutes.—The minutes were afterwards pissed.

MEDICAL OPPICIDE'S REPORT. Dr. Watkins submitted his report for the year 1894 , —Births, males 234, females 237, total 471; deaths, males 73, females 83, total 156. The birth rate was 344, and the general death rate 11.3 per 1,000 of the estimated population. The infant death rate under one year of age per thousand births registered was 10.4, 7 deaths resulting front injuries, 1 of a stranger, and the death of another person not be'onging to the district, reduced the net total death rate from disease to 10.8 per 1,000. The death rate from all infectious diseases coming to the medical officer's knowledge was 1.1, and the sick rate 5.7 per 1,000 of the estimated population. The deaths of chil- dren under five years of age were 42.3 of the total num- ber of deaths. Seventy-five out of 156 deaths might be classified according to the certificates of death, i.e., scarlatina 2, diphtheria 3, croup 2, enteric or typhoid fever 4. puerperal fever 2, cholera nostras 1, whooping cough 1, diarrhoea 1, rheumatic fever 1, plithisis 8, bronchitis, pneumonia, and pleurisy 34 (exactly half of them in the last quarter of the year), heart disease 9, injuries 7. There were 79 new cases of infectious sick- ness notified :—Scarlatina 35 (21 of them in the last , quarter of the year), diphtheria 13, ensteric or typhoid 1 fever 12, puerperal fever 2, erysipelas 17. The case of cholera nostras which occurred in May was not notified In the life time of patient; the duration of the attack was certified to have been 24 days. Nine of these cases were isolated in the infectious diseases hospital at War- rington. It was much to be regretted that greater ad- vantage was not taken of the Councll's contract with the Warrington Corporation. It would at least diminish the number of foci of contagion, and it would prevent such centres of infection, as a small cottage with four cases of scarlet fever, in it at the same time. Be advised the Council to press upon his professional brethren how necersary it was for the safety of their neighbours to have all suitable cases removed. Noti- fication was an invaluable aid in dealing with infec- tious diseases,but it was an incomplete safeguard whilst Isolation was so much neglected. The district was under his constant observation, and he was of opinion that Igenerally there was an increased knowledgelamongst the people of the influence of their environments on them, land the steady effort to improve it. This was notice- able among the Vulcan Cottages, where the company had done much sanitary work in the past year. The water supply was good and plentiful, bet the pressure was somewhat variable and defective in the higher parts of the township, which would be a most serious matter in the event of a fire. The scavenging was done by the Sanitary Authority, and not by contract,and he believed , it to be as well done as circumstances would permit. The night soil was too often allowed to accu- mulate in too close proximity to the public thorough...l fare and footpaths. The refuse, too, was secesuarily deposited in various parts of the district. It was rapidly and literally becoming a burning question, and the solution of it was increasingly urgent, as the natural increase of the population was much in excess of the estimated increase. Newton lake remained in ranch the sarae state as last reported upon, the main affluent bringing down the chief pollution. There had,however, been some improvement lately, and he certainly hoped for a further improvement in the future. It was par- ticularly gratifying to him to make such a report as that to the new Council.—The Chairman said the report was a most satisfactory one. In the returns of the County Council they stood 2 per cent, below the healthiest towns in the county. He moved the adoption of the report.—Mr. Smith seconded, and suggested that the report he entered on the minutes.—Mr. Gilmour said that whilst the doctor was reading the report, one of his colleagues remarked, " Wargrave again. fle should like to know from the doctor his opinien—if there were more deaths in Wargrave tlian in any other die- trict.—Dr. Watkins said it was not deaths, but cases he was reading out.—Tie Chairman said he did not think they need take any notice of any casual remark they heard. He should like to know what the question was. —Mr. Gilmour said the question was whether War- grave was more unhealthy than any other district.—Dr. Watkins observed that Mr.Gilnaour was labouring under a wrong impression when he used the word "deaths."— Mr. Gilmour said he referred to disease.—Dr. Watkins said the incidence of disease in Wargrave Ward was 20 out of 79.—The report was adopted.

At a meeting of the Finance Committee held January 21st, accounts amounting to £l,OlO 17s. ld. were passed for payment. Messrs. Tau Smoot DITPFICULTT.—The excitement occasioned by the dacision of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. to close the infant portban of Blackhrook British Schools, leaving the infant children of Nirmoriformists no other alternative but to attend the now Parish Church Schools has not subsided. A letter of sympathy with the local Congregationalists having been received from Miss Ruth Evans, of Rhyl, the following resolution was passed on Sunday niztit, after the or hurry service in the Con- gregational Chapel :—" That this mceting of flaydock Congregationalists desires hereby to express to Miss Ruth Evans its grateful fine hearty appreciation of her kind sympathy wit k them under the grave injustice which they, in common with ether Nonconformists in the town, will suff...r by the clueing of the Blackeronit British Infant School. .It dasires to thank Miss Evans for the great interest which shf3 has always shown in the highest welfare ot the children, and to record its entire satisfaction both with the teaching staff and the general administration, especially with the unsectarian character of the religious instruction imparted to the scholars, during the many years that the school was under her wise and liberal management. It is the earnest and sincere prayer of this meeting that Miss Evans may continue to enjoy the richest blessings of Hint for the promotion of whose glory she has made so many and such noble sacrifices."

OLD LADIES' TEA PARTY.—An excellent tea was pro- vided to about 50 of the aged women in the village on Friday night. The following ladies presided at the tables: —Mrs. Wray, Miss Johnston, Mrs. T. Wright, Mrs. Had- dock and Miss Cissie Stokes, assisted by Mrs. Walter Collier (Runcern), Miss Stokes, Miss L. Wright, Miss Elsie Wright, Mies Barbara Johnson, Miss Jones, and others. After tea the Vicar gave a very stirring address, Mr. Stokes also gave them some very good advise. The Vicar proposed athearty vote of thanks to Mr. and Mrs, 'T. Wright, who took so much trouble to make the annual gathering a success. A musical programme was afterwards gone through. Mr. Wright suitably replied. About eleven o'clock a packet of tea was presented to each guest, and the singing of " Auld Lang Syne " brought so enjoyable evening to a close. OLD MEN'S SUPPER.—At the Norton Arms Hotel, on Wednesday evening, the 27th anniversary of the Old Men's supper was held, when about 50 guests whose ages ranged from 59 to 76, were present. Many of the oldest men were unable to be present owing to the severe weather, but these will not be neglected. The guests partook of a substantial supper served by the host and hostess, Mr. and Mrs. Birch. After supper several toasts were proposed and duly honoured. Songs were afterwards given by the Rev. G. D. VC ray, Mr. Billington, Mr. Painter, and Mr. Dutton. Mrs.sWray played the accompaniment. The guests sign'fied their • thanks by hearty cheers.

THE ALLEGED SERIOUS ASSAULT. THE INJT2RED MAN IMPROVING. BAIL ALLOWED. There was a large number of people at the Borough Police Court on Monday morning when William Broad- hurst, a young man, and labourer at Messrs. Bylan da Brothers wireworks, and residing at 22, General-street, VVarritagton, was charged before the Mayor (Mr. James Fairclough), Messrs. Heyward, Monks, and i rierpoint, with doing grievous bodily harm to Edward Allen, twenty-four years if age, a 1 labourer at the same works, and residing at 5, Derby- street, off Hopwood-stroet. Inspector Spinks said Deteetive-sergeant Mormon and himself had learned from inquiries that some disturbance, the nature if which they were unable to get at,occurred a little betore Isix o'clock on Saturday night in Crossley-street. The I defendant and the injured man, who was then uacon- scious, went down Crosaley-street, and at the junction of Brick-street and Crossley-street at a beerhouse there, kept by ansan named Russell, they were seen leaning on a window-sill. A man came up at the time and heard angry words passing between them. It is alleged that presently the defendant was seen to bump Allen's head against the window, throw him down, his head striking the parapet, and when he was down, kick him on the mouth (Prisoner : " It is false "). Broadhurst ran away when the cry of " Murder" was raised. Witness visited several houses, and about two o'clock on Sunday morn- ing visited defendant's* house and asked if his name was Broadhurst, and tisld him that it was alleged he was concerned in a disturtanee In Crossley-street on Saturday night, and that if he knew anything about it he had better tell him. Broadhurst then replied, "I know nothing about it, I have not seen Allen since Friday. Additional informa- tion was received, and witness returned later and took Broadhurst into custody. Broadhurst said," I wish you had come at tea o'elock. I wish I had told you all about it when you were here. I hit him because he was choking me." On the way to the police station he said he would like to see the injured man, but witness told him that he had not regained camsciousness, and that the doctor would not allow anyone to see him. The affair occurred about six on Saturday night, and Allen had regained consciousness three or four times, but only for two or three minutes at a time. Witness having asked if he should tell the court the extent of the in- juries, Mr. White (magistrates' clerk) said the length of the remand should depend on the extent of these in- juries. The Mayor asked if the doctor said there was any hope of Allen's recovery. Witness replied " None whatever (sensation in court.) His skull is fractured." A. remand for forty-eight hours was granted. Prisoner : Can Ibe allowed bail—The Chairman : No the case is too serious ; the man might die in the meantime.—Mr. F. Monks Then it would be a case of manslaughter. Prisoner was then conducted below. WEDNESDAY'S PROCEEDINGS. On Wednesday morning befell, Mr. John Fairclough (chairman), Mr. J. H. Fleming and Mr. J. Geddes, the Berne charge was read over to the prisoner who appeared to be very pale and ill. Mr. A. Browne appeared to re- present the prisoner. Dr. McCarthy stated that he was called in on Saturday evening to see Idles. and found him suffering frem wounds cn the head, contusion of the month, and he had been bleedings great deal from the nose. He had been uncenscious until Tuesday morning. rie had also had several convulsions. Witness saw the injured man last, on Wednesday morning, and he was then going on very favoJrahly hut was not o'i'. of danger. The other injuries were fractures of the have of the skull and a slight scalp wound almost healed. Mr. Hunt (chief constable), applied for a remand of eight days to allow of the injured man's iurner recovery. Mr. Brownu had no objection to the remand but he applied for bail. His client, he said, was Warrington born and had served his time at IMPSSIE. Relands' Bros., and had an •xcellent character. Several of his relations were in court, and he was there to say that if bail were granted his client would appear at the time fixed. His instructions were that the case was not so serious as WAS at first I height, and he had witnesses to prove that the man was not kicked as at first supposed. Under these circumstances there should be no objection to granting Mr. Bunt said that so far as was consistent with his duty he was agreeable to the remand, but opposed to !sail, as one of his chief witnesses had been tampered with. Mr. Browne stated that his client did not deny that 1 he had struck Allen one blow, but that was in conse- quence of what the latter had done to him. He (Mr. Browne) did not know anything about the alleged tampering, and hoped that it was untrue. As there was a serious accusation against his client, Mr. Browne thought it was only fair that the young man should lse " out." to prepare his defence, an prove to Warrington and their Worships that he was not guilty of inflicting grevious bodily harm upon Allen. Mr. Browne an- noueced that Dr. M'Carthv had just told him that there were no signs of nicking about Allen's body. The Beech, at the request of Dr. M'Carthy, remanded the case until Tuesday, the 19 h of the present month, and gran:ed prisoner bail—himself in £5O and his 'ather, William Broadhurst, and Mr. Woistenholme, of .he Manx Arms, in the sum of £25 each.

div.head: SERVICE OF SONG.
div.p: SERVICE OF SONG.

On Saturday night the St. Peter's Church Young Women's Bible Class gave a service of song entitled "Christy's Old Organ, in the Workingmen's Gospel Temperance Mission Hall. Mrs. 'Willis presided, and opened the proceedings by delivering an able address on the subject of temperance. Owing to the sad bereavement which Mrs. Percival has sus- tained in the death of her father, this lady was unable to give the reading as was anticipated. Her place, however, was taken by the Rev. J. Cooil, anrate of St. Peter's, who gave the readings in an cppropriate style.

GENERAL NEWS. Lamereably great as the number of the victims of the disaster to the Elbe still is, it is now found not to be so high as was at first anticipated. After the steamer went down the number of the dro.aned was estimated at 380. A careful revisisn of the lists of the passengers and crew has enabled the North German Lloyd Coin. pany to state positively that it cannot exceed 335. The police of Berlin have discovered several secret manufactories of rifle cartridges in that city. It is be- lieved the cartridges were being manufactured for the Chinese Government. The Chelford disaster deatb-zoll has now been brought up to fourteen by the death at Crewe on Monday of Mr. Albert Pitcher, of Old Trafford, who sustained severe internal injuries on the occasion of the collision. The fourth of the representative matches between Mr. Stoddart's team and " All Australia" ended at Sydney on Monday in defeat for the Englishmen by an innings and 147 runs. The visitors found themselves compelled to meet on a wicket which had been thoroughly ruined by rain, some of the best bowlers in the world, and defeat was inevitable. Each side has now won two matches, and enormous interest will attach to the filth and last which will be played at Melbourne. It is calculated that if the children under the care of the London ;••chool Hoard were to join hands they would reach from London to Carlisle, a distance of three hundred mars. Intense cold prevailed in Liverpool and the neighbour- hood on Tuesday, the frost during the night having been probably the severest of the season. At Market Har- borough on Tuesday 30 degrees of frost are stated to have been registered. A Pendletou cattle drover named Harry Harrison.was gored to death by a bull in the Salford Cattle Marl, et,c n , Tuesday.
